SATOM — User Guide

Audience: operators and network/security engineers who use the web UI to manage FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer appliances day to day, and to read FortiGate configuration. No knowledge of the codebase is assumed. For architecture and internals see the Engineering Manual; for a non-technical summary see the Management Overview.

1. Signing in & accounts

  • Browse to the app URL and log in. A fresh install seeds one administrator, admin, with no default password: it is the one given to the installer (--admin-password=… / SATOM_ADMIN_PASSWORD) or a random one the installer writes to initial-admin-password in the install directory (root-only, 0600; the installer prints its path). Change it on first login (Profile → password) and delete that file.
  • Account protection: 10 consecutive failed logins lock the account for 15 minutes. Login attempts are rate-limited per IP (5/min).
  • 2FA: TOTP can be enabled per account, with QR enrollment on Settings → Security. Enabling it issues backup codes that are shown exactly once — save them then; you can regenerate a fresh set later, which immediately invalidates the old one. Set a recovery email on the same tab if you want Forgot password to be able to reach you (§26.13).
  • Directory auth: LDAP and RADIUS backends are configured at Settings → Authentication (§26.7), alongside local accounts. That tab also tests the connection against unsaved form values, and syncs directory users into local rows so an admin can assign a profile before first sign-in — synced accounts are created disabled, pending approval.
  • Who can reach the app at all is a separate question from who can sign in: Settings → Access Control (§26.2) carries an IP whitelist. It means everywhere when left empty, and loopback and admins are always allowed so it cannot lock you out. There is no per-username allowlist any more — the directory group, the approval gate and the profile already decide that.
  • Roles. Three effective profiles ship, and they gate what you can do:
  • readonly — see everything, change nothing;
  • operator — day-to-day changes (config_write): policies, objects, exceptions, backups;
  • admin (user_manage) — everything, including Settings, users, registry, templates, scheduled actions, and the Database section.

These three are seeded, not a closed set. Settings → Profiles (§26.3) composes profiles freely from the granular permission catalog, so a profile that can, say, use the Lua Studio but not administer users is a configuration, not a feature request. - Every write you make is recorded in the Audit Log with before/after change history. - Documentation and API documentation, under the sign-in form, open the manual this node serves itself — no internet needed, no sign-in needed (§47).

2. Core concepts

DB-first pages. The app keeps a local, queryable copy of each device's whole configuration (populated by Rediscovery and Deep Capture). Pages render from that cache in milliseconds and show a freshness badge like DB · 2h ago. This means:

  • the UI works even when a device is down, slow, or license-locked;
  • what you see can be behind the box — press the refresh/live control (⟳ / "refresh from device") when you need the current truth. A refresh is a full device sync, so it needs config_write on every page that offers it (Server Policy, Server Objects, Web Protection, the configuration sections); read-only users see the cached data and no refresh button;
  • after you save a change through the app, the affected page re-reads live, so your own edits are never stale.

Dry-run first. Every write to a device shows a preview (exactly what will be PUT/POSTed) before you apply. Nothing touches an appliance until you explicitly confirm. Applied writes are snapshotted and audited.

Jobs dock. Long operations (backups, discovery, deep captures, bulk applies, firmware) run as background jobs. A dock at the bottom of the screen tracks progress and survives page navigation; the Jobs page (Global → Jobs) lists everything with Pause / Resume / Stop. Each toast in the dock can be minimised to one line (−) and restored (□, or a click on its title); the choice lasts for the browser session.

Notifications. The bell in the top bar collects job results and system notices, scoped to the product you are working in. The bell's Clear only marks them read; Clear all on the Notifications page deletes them (after a confirmation).

The names, in the industry's words. SATOM is mapped to the NAF Framework, the Network Automation Forum's vendor-neutral model of a network automation system (six blocks: Intent, Executor, Collector, Observability, Orchestrator, Presentation). If you know that model, read SATOM's names like this: the Source of Truth and the device cache are Observability (the actual state and its history), Templates and Baselines are Intent (the desired state), Rediscovery / Deep Capture / metrics collection are the Collector, every device write is the Executor, Processes, Scheduled Actions and Change Requests are the Orchestrator, and this console, the CLI and the API are Presentation. The full naming table, the source and the conformance matrix are in SATOM and the NAF Framework.

3. Products (ADOMs)

The app currently hosts six workspaces, in the style of FortiManager ADOMs. The list is data, not code: the ADOM registry is a database table, and an admin creates, renames, reorders, deactivates or deletes workspaces at Settings → ADOMs (§26.11) — including which shared capabilities (banner, API tokens, firmware, naming, regex) each one offers. global, fortiweb and fortiadc are the exception: their keys are wired into URL scoping, so they can be deactivated but not deleted. What you see below is this installation's current list:

ADOM URL Purpose
Global / Fleet-wide dashboard and cross-product tools: Monitoring (with Metrics and Analysis), Search, Service Diagram, Architecture, Fleet Objects, WAF, Jobs, DNS Lookup, and an Automation sub-menu (with Certificate Manager, and an API sub-menu holding Schema builds and Build compatibility); and fleet administration under Administrator, in sections (Access, Change Management, Devices, Objects, Studio, System)
FortiWeb /web/ Everything WAF: FortiWeb's own menu for the selected device (Policy, Server Objects, Web Protection, System, …), the device-scoped WAF tools under Operations → WAF (Search Attack ID, Exceptions & Signature, WAF Artifacts), Operations, FortiWeb administration
FortiADC /adc/ Load-balancer management: the device's own menu when a layout exists for its build (otherwise a FortiADC group with Signatures only), and an ADC API console
FortiAuthenticator /fac/ Identity and access: the unit's own menu (users and groups, RADIUS and TACACS+ clients, Fortinet SSO, certificates…) drawn from its measured GUI, and a FAC API console
FortiAnalyzer /faz/ Logging and analytics: the device's own menu when a layout exists for its build (otherwise the curated menu: Device Manager, FortiView, Log View, Incidents & Events, Reports), and a JSON-RPC API console
FortiGate /fgt/ Next-generation firewall: the FortiOS menu of the selected unit — Network, Policy & Objects, Security Profiles, VPN, User & Authentication, Security Fabric, System, Log & Report — read live over the REST API, with dry-run-first writes on the pages a measured layout draws (§17.4)

The Global dashboard is where every session starts: the health of SATOM's own infrastructure (the HA nodes, the code repository, the backup server), one tile per ADOM with its appliance count, the Jobs and Certificates tiles, and a row of shortcuts to the global sections. A tile opens that ADOM.

The Global dashboard: infrastructure health, one tile per ADOM, and the global sections.

Each product workspace mirrors its appliance's own GUI menu, so an operator who knows the device knows where to look. How that menu is built differs by product (§3.2); §17 covers what each workspace adds beyond the shared pages.

Switch ADOMs from the product selector or the ‹ Global link at the top of each sidebar. The ADOM is per browser tab — you can keep FortiWeb open in one tab and FortiADC in another; switching in one tab never changes the other. Data is strictly scoped: a FortiADC session sees only FortiADC jobs, notifications, templates and appliances (and vice versa); Global sees all.

A profile can be confined to some ADOMs (§26.3). Then the selector and the sidebar offer only those ADOMs, opening another one is refused, and the Global console shows the union of them — their devices, records, jobs and counters — never the whole fleet.

3.1 The selected device is per ADOM

Most per-device pages read an implicit device context rather than asking which appliance you mean on every page. That context is one slot per ADOM: picking a FortiWeb on the Service Diagram and picking a FortiAuthenticator on the FAC dashboard are two independent choices, and neither disturbs the other. The Global console reads FortiWeb's slot, as it always has.

An ADOM that holds exactly one appliance does not ask. With no choice to make, that appliance is the context on every page of the ADOM — the dashboard and the menu alike. It is a resolution, not a selection: nothing is written to your session, so the picker still shows what you actually chose and the Select button still means something. From two appliances up, the choice is real and the pages ask for it.

An appliance in maintenance mode is counted only for operators who may see maintenance devices, so this can never hand you a device the picker hides.

3.2 The device menu: drawn from the device's own GUI

In the FortiWeb, FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator, FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer ADOMs the sidebar has one device menu, named after the product, and it is the device's own menu: the groups, sub-menus and pages the Fortinet GUI shows, in the device's order. SATOM does not keep a menu of its own for these products. It builds the menu from the GUI layouts measured on real firmware builds, which reach the node through the knowledge packs (§22.4), so the menu follows the selected device (§3.1):

  • Per firmware build. Each page uses the layout measured on the device's exact build, else the same version, else the same train, else the closest older train. The page header says which build the layout comes from (with a knowledge pack badge) and warns when it is not the device's own.
  • Only pages the build has. When the device's own build was measured, a page that only another build's menu has is left out unless that build was measured serving the page's collections. A build nobody measured shows every page of the nearest layout, since leaving pages out by measurement would empty its menu.
  • All pages, the first entry of the group, opens a grid with every page in the device's menu order, one card per top-level group.
  • A knowledge pack that brings new layouts shows up in the menu within about a minute (the menu is cached for 60 seconds per product and build).

FortiWeb ADOM, device fwb-01: the FortiWeb group is FortiWeb's own menu; All pages lists every page by group.

Pages open SATOM's GUI pages (/workspace/<id>/fwgui/<page>): the device's structure (tabs, columns, dialogs and fields, with their show/hide rules) inside the SATOM frame, and the SATOM tools on top. FortiWeb's Server Policy keeps its own hand-tuned view (§5).

The old SATOM menus are gone. The FortiWeb ADOM no longer draws the Loadbalancer (Server Objects), WAF (Web Protection Profile, Web Protection, the protection areas) and Configuration groups, and the FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs no longer draw their former SATOM section menus. The Classic view button is gone from every list and settings page too. What moved and what did not:

  • Bookmarks keep working. An old URL for a collection that a measured page draws redirects to that page.
  • Collections no measured page draws yet have no menu entry. They come back as their pages are measured and arrive in a knowledge pack. A bookmark to such a page still opens it.
  • FortiWeb WAF tools — Search Attack ID, Exceptions & Signature and WAF Artifacts — are now under Operations → WAF (§9). They are drawn in every device ADOM, in the same place; outside FortiWeb they are greyed out and say why on hover. The URLs and permissions are the same.

When there is nothing to draw. In the FortiWeb ADOM, with no device selected or no layout imported for it yet (fresh install, offline node, no knowledge pack), the FortiWeb group keeps one entry, Server Policy. It opens the device's Server Policy view, SATOM's own Server Policy list with a notice when no layout exists, or the Service Diagram, where you pick a device, when none is selected. The FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs draw no device group in that case. Their dashboards, the page each ADOM opens on, still list SATOM's section pages (§17.2, §17.4).

FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer draw their own menu only where a layout exists. A FortiADC or FortiAnalyzer whose firmware build has a measured layout in the knowledge packs gets the device's menu like the other three. Otherwise a FortiADC keeps a FortiADC group with Signatures only, and a FortiAnalyzer keeps the curated menu of §17.3 (the live JSON-RPC section pages), so neither ADOM ends up empty.

Where the shared groups sit. Every device ADOM draws the same SATOM groups in the same order around the device menu: Operations first, the device menu, Administrator, Plugins. Operations opens with the fleet pages (Dashboard where the ADOM has one, Calendar, Architecture, Service Diagram, Monitoring, Search, DNS Lookup, Troubleshooting, Fleet Objects and WAF in FortiWeb and FortiADC, Jobs), then holds Device Backups and Import Backup, and ends with the Automation sub-menu; Diagnose Log Collection is in Operations › Troubleshooting (§27). There is no separate Fleet group, and no separate Automation group in a device ADOM (the Global ADOM draws Automation as a sub-menu of its Global block, above Jobs). The API sub-menu of Automation holds the console (Registry & console, device ADOMs) and Schema builds and Build compatibility (every ADOM, Global included). System Automations is in Settings → System; Automation keeps Automations, the work operators schedule (§15). Appliances is under Administrator; Certificate Manager is under Automation (Certificate Manager in every ADOM: live in Global, FortiWeb and FortiADC, drawn disabled with the reason in FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator). Administrator is split into sections — Access, Change Management, Devices, Objects, Studio and System — and both the sections and their entries are alphabetical in the console's language; a section with no entry you may open is not drawn. Studio holds Python Studio (the Script Library and the Python console in one page, §23.3) in every ADOM, and also Plugin Studio and Lua Studio in Global. The Global ADOM keeps its Global block for the fleet pages and has no Operations group. A profile that cannot see one of those groups keeps the entry where it was before — Appliances under Operations, the API menu (console, Schema builds, Build compatibility) as a group of its own in a device ADOM and inside the Global block in Global (registry.view without config_write), Studio as a group of its own, and Process in a group of its own — so the reorder takes no page away from anyone. Each entry keeps its own permission; moving it changed where it is drawn, not who sees it.

The Global ADOM has no device menu. It is the fleet-wide console. Its Operations → WAF lists the fleet pages (Overview, Inventory, Profiles, Coverage, Artifacts, Exceptions) but not the three FortiWeb tools above. Those are FortiWeb-ADOM pages, and a link from Global would switch the tab's ADOM without saying so.

4. Registering and operating devices

Appliances (sidebar → Operations → Appliances in each ADOM, Global → Appliances in the Global ADOM, or the Global dashboard). The entry is shown to anyone holding appliances.view; adding or editing a device still needs config_write:

  1. Add appliance — name, host/IP, port, kind (fortiweb / fortiadc / fortiauthenticator / fortianalyzer / fortigate), credentials (stored encrypted), TLS verification mode.

If a new appliance never syncs, check TLS verification first. An appliance that presents a self-signed certificate fails CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED before it ever authenticates, so the row sits at unknown forever with credentials that are perfectly good. Either import its CA under Settings → Trust store, or set verification off for that device. This is the single most common cause of a brand-new device that will not come online.

FortiAuthenticator authenticates with a per-user API key, not the login password: issue one by ticking Web service access on an Administrator account on the unit, and store that key as the appliance password. FortiGate likewise takes a REST API administrator token (execute api-user generate-key <api-user> on the FortiGate) as the password, never a login password; a read-only admin profile is enough (§17.4).

Editing an appliance keeps its stored credentials, which nobody can read back. Changing its host, port, username or platform — or turning its TLS verification off — therefore needs the password entered again in the same save (and the SSH password too when the device has a separate one); otherwise the save is refused. The same rule applies to PUT /api/appliances/<id>.

SSH credentials, when they differ from the API ones. The Edit page has two optional fields for the CLI login. Use SSH user, if different from the API user when the API user cannot open SSH. A FortiGate registered with a REST api-user is the usual case. Use SSH password, if different from the API credential when the stored password is an API key, as on FortiAuthenticator. Left empty, SSH logs in with the API username and password. Diagnose Log Collection and Diagnostic Battery discovery (§27) log in with this SSH user and SSH password, and the other read-only SSH sessions also log in as the SSH user. If you change the SSH user while a separate SSH password is stored, enter that password again in the same save (or remove it), as for a username change.

SNMP polling (opt-in). The Edit page also carries the snmp collector's switch, port (161) and community string — stored like the passwords, never shown again, removable with its checkbox. Enabling it needs a community string; it provisions the snmp scrape target at once, and switching it off disables that target. What is polled and what the appliance must allow is in §14.7. 2. Test connection — validates REST reachability and credentials. 3. Discovery / Rediscovery — sweeps every registry endpoint and stores the device's full configuration in the local cache (recorded as a harvest with trigger rediscovery, so Device health counts it); also records the firmware. Hardware is NOT collected here: use Scan hardware (SSH) on Device health (FortiWeb only: the scan is the FortiWeb diagnose hardware battery, so the button is not offered in the other ADOMs). Run it after registering and after any large out-of-band change. With Capture full WPP + policy depth on, the deep pass shows which server policy or WPP it is walking and how many are left. 4. Deep capture — a deeper sweep that walks each server policy's whole object graph (pools, members, WAF profile sub-policies…). This is what powers the DB-first policy detail and the Service Diagram. Can run fleet-wide and is normally scheduled nightly. 5. Factory catalog (the device's Web Protection Profile list in the FortiWeb menu → Factory catalog, or Template Library → Factory catalog; needs View registry) — the FortiWeb predefined Web Protection Profiles, stored once per firmware version, build number and REST API version. The first deep pass on a build reads them in full; later deep passes rebuild a predefined profile from the catalog when the appliance's own rows match, and read it in full again once a week. Turn on Re-read predefined WPPs in full on the Rediscovery page to read them now. On the catalog page you can open a profile's full tree, compare the same profile between two builds (what the vendor changed in its defaults), and save an entry as a template, stamped with that firmware and API version.

Each appliance's detail page is the hub for device-level actions:

  • VS/Policy Inspector — a tree report of each policy and everything it references.
  • SSH Console — read-only troubleshooting presets (get system status, HA status, routing table, sniffer…) plus a command box. Destructive CLI is not offered. Only get, show and diagnose are accepted. A diagnose command whose name changes the device (kill, clear, reset, delete, failover, sysrq/crash, set, enable/disable, format…) is refused, including abbreviations such as diag sys kil. Running a command (even a read-only one) needs Run appliance actions (appliances.apply); without it the console link is not shown and the page lists the presets with a read-only notice.
  • Backups / Restore / Upgrade / Boot partition — see §11–§12.
  • Sync devices — the fleet list can be shared/re-imported so a fresh install inherits the same inventory.

Capacity limits (Administrator → Capacity) define per-model object ceilings; clone and exception workflows check headroom before creating objects.

Every action on a device is a job. Test connection, console commands, restores, failovers, saves in the Workspace and the object editor, certificate pushes, searches on the box: each one runs in the background and shows what it is doing.

  • An action that finishes within about two seconds behaves as it always did.
  • A longer one appears in the Jobs dock (bottom right) with each call it makes to the device, for example GET /api/v2.0/cmdb/server-policy/policy · 200 · 310 ms. The page gets its normal result when the action ends, even if you went to another page in the meantime.
  • A form you submitted opens a progress page with the same steps. Keep working takes you back; the action continues.
  • Two changes to the same device run one after the other. The second shows queued and can be stopped while it waits. Once a change has started on the device it cannot be stopped, so the device is never left half-changed.
  • The appliance page has a Jobs on this device card with the running and recent jobs; every job is also on Global → Jobs, with its steps under Details.

5. Server Policy

FortiWeb ADOM → sidebar group FortiWeb → Server Policy (the device's own menu, §3). The page is drawn in FortiWeb's own layout for the device's firmware build: the same toolbar, the same columns in the same order and the same row behaviour as the appliance GUI, inside the SATOM frame. The layout comes from the knowledge packs (§7.4 explains the banner above the table).

Server Policy on fwb-01: FortiWeb's toolbar plus the SATOM actions, and the cache badge.

  • Rows come from the SATOM cache of the device, not from a live read. The badge at the right of the toolbar says when the cache was taken; ⟳ (Refresh) pulls the live configuration from the device and returns to this list (it needs config_write). The VIP and Port columns are joined from the policy's deep capture; a policy without one shows — there.
  • Click a row to select it; double-click, Enter or Edit opens it. Tick the checkboxes (or the one in the header for every visible row) to select several: the actions below then run on all of them, and Edit needs exactly one.
  • Search filters the visible rows by name (plain text or /regex/). Filters below the toolbar adds VIP / IP, backend pool, backend server IP, certificate type and status; the VIP and backend filters read the deep capture.
  • A policy that was cloned or migrated carries a copies badge beside its name; hover it for each copy, where it landed, when, by whom, and the reason of an attempt that failed.
  • Create New opens FortiWeb's Create New menu. An entry marked conditional may be hidden on this device by a setting SATOM cannot see. The form starts with FortiWeb's own defaults; a policy with no HTTP, HTTPS or HTTP/3 service is refused before anything is written, the preview included. If any step of the create fails, the objects that run created are deleted again, newest first, and the result lists what was undone.

Toolbar actions on the selected policy

FortiWeb's toolbar is extended with SATOM's policy actions. Each one acts on the selected rows and always shows a dry-run preview before anything is written:

Button What it does
Clone Deep-clones the policy tree on this FortiWeb under a new name (§6).
Clone to Deep-clones the policy tree onto another FortiWeb (§6).
Migrate to Clones onto another FortiWeb and, only if that lands cleanly, disables the source. The source is never deleted (§6).
Enable / Disable Turns the policy on or off. Disable stops the traffic and keeps the object.
Delete Safe cascade: the policy plus only the objects nothing else uses. Web Protection Profiles, certificates, services and shared objects are kept, and the preview lists both.

The six actions open SATOM's policy dialog on this page. Its options, preview and background job are the ones described in §6. A link to …/workspace/<id>?act=<action>&policy=<name> opens the list with that dialog already open for that policy. Clone to and Migrate to stay disabled while no other FortiWeb is registered. A user without config_write sees the list without the action buttons.

The page header adds two buttons:

  • From a line profile — the wizard in §5.1 (needs config_write).
  • Change Appliance — back to the device picker.

Editing a policy

Edit opens FortiWeb's Edit Server Policy dialog for the policy's protocol, with the device's own sections, sub-dialogs and inline tables:

  • Fields show and hide as you edit, as FortiWeb's GUI does (§7.4).
  • Rows of the inline tables open in their own dialog. Create New is offered in a table's toolbar only when SATOM knows that sub-table and can read its rows; a table SATOM cannot read is never written blind.
  • The pencil beside a reference selector (Virtual Server, Server Pool, HTTP Service…) opens the selected object in a panel stacked over the dialog; Esc closes it.
  • Below the dialog, Not in GUI, but in CLI lists every field this policy has on the device's build that FortiWeb's GUI does not show (§7.6).
  • Save works as described in §7.5: you review the change first, then apply it. Before the write, the dialog runs the same checks as the object editor: a template-managed Web Protection Profile stays read-only, another user's edit lease blocks the save, every reference value is checked against the device (§7.1) and the build compatibility check runs (§7.3). After a successful write, SATOM reads the policy back from the device so the page shows the stored value.

Without a knowledge pack

When no FortiWeb GUI layout has been imported on this node yet (a fresh install, or the knowledge feed switched off) the list still opens, with a note saying so: FortiWeb 7.6's default columns, the same toolbar actions and filters. Create New then opens SATOM's New Server Policy form and Edit opens SATOM's policy view: rendered from the deep cache with the resolved service topology (VIP + port → virtual server → pool → real servers), Check live health for the real per-backend health-check state, and a minimal-diff edit form with a ＋ next to creatable references.

The old SATOM list at /web/workspace/<id> is gone; the address now opens this list (an act/policy deep link included).

To enable or disable a policy or a backend, change a backend's IP or port, or swap a policy's certificate at a set date and time, use a Scheduled Action (§15).

5.1 New Server Policy from a line — the wizard

/web/workspace/<id>/spo-wizard, reached from the From a line profile button in the Server Policy page header.

You pick a line, and its profile supplies the network segment, the certificate class and the Web Protection Profile. The wizard then runs the whole chain in one order: IPAM reserves the VIP, DNS publishes the name, the CA issues the certificate, and the device gets the objects. The point of the wizard is not speed — it is that a failure halfway through this chain strands a reserved address and an issued certificate that nobody finds by looking at the appliance.

Preview writes nothing. Preview builds a plan and returns every reason the run cannot proceed, not just the first. It reserves no address, creates no record, issues no certificate and touches the device only to read it, so it is safe to press at any time and at any permission level that can already see the device. Apply is the only button that writes, and it needs config_write.

A blocked plan is never applied — dry run included. There is no "just to preview it" path past a blocker; allowing one is how a blocker becomes advisory.

The name collision is checked live, against the device. The derived object names are compared with the appliance's own object list at plan time, not with a cached copy — a run that dies after reserving an address is worse than one that never started. An unreachable device is itself a blocker, not an assumption that the box is empty. The same live read confirms that the line's Web Protection Profile exists on the device; a missing profile blocks the plan (deploy the template first) instead of failing at the last step.

Names follow Administrator → Naming. Object names are rendered from the saved Naming patterns and variables for the device's product (§13.3), falling back to the defaults for any element left empty. When the wizard issues a certificate, the created policy serves HTTPS with it (predefined HTTPS service + that certificate).

The port of each domain goes into {port} in the names. Each domain row has a Port column, and a flow that creates policies through the wizard's API passes port per domain. Left blank, the port written in the address is used (shop.example.com:8443); with none there, 443 when the policy carries a certificate and 80 when it does not, and the plan warns that a name carries a port nobody typed. The preview prints the four derived names and where the port came from (given, from the address, default). A name with a character the devices refuse (anything but letters, digits, _ and -; a dot from {host} is the usual one) blocks the plan as naming_unsafe. Rewrite it with a variable.

A segment can hold several networks. On Network Segments each segment lists one or more networks (CIDR + gateway, optionally an interface of its own; blank uses the segment's interface). With Reserve the VIP from IPAM, the VIP is taken from the first network with a free address: if IPAM refuses one (full, or any other error) the next is tried, and the address step says which networks refused and why. The preview lists the order. A network no IPAM backend can serve is reported as a warning ("will NOT be tried"); only when none can be used does the plan block. The VIP goes on the interface of the network it came from, and an address released after a later failure goes back to that same network. A VIP typed by hand must sit in one of the segment's networks (address_not_in_segment otherwise; {ip}/24 is accepted). The gateway is recorded with each network; no flow writes it to the device. Segments saved before this change read as one network, unchanged, and a CIDR the page cannot parse drops that network only, never the segment.

Line profiles are declared on Global ADOM → Administrator → Line Profiles and are always filed as FortiWeb profiles — the product the wizard reads them for.

It refuses to guess. A segment the chosen line does not receive is refused — the wrong-network failure this feature exists to prevent. When a line offers several segments you choose one; the wizard does not pick for you. A blank hostname means do not publish and never quietly becomes the web address. A backend that cannot write records, plus a requested hostname, is a refusal — not a step that reports success and publishes nothing.

On failure, what was undone and what was left behind are reported as separate lists. Compensation is driven by what the run recorded, never by inspecting the current state of the world:

  • A DNS failure releases the address by its handle, and only if IPAM handed it out. A hand-typed VIP is not SATOM's to hand back to a pool.
  • A device failure removes the record this run created and releases the address this run took.
  • An issued certificate is named and NOT revoked. Revocation is destructive and irreversible, and a certificate that exists is not harmful.
  • Objects already written to the device are listed, not deleted. Deleting one that a human may already have bound elsewhere is a destructive guess.

The result keeps compensated ("we undid this") and stranded ("we did not undo this") as two lists and renders them separately, because they are opposite facts and folding them would let a leftover read as a cleanup. The certificate is deliberately in the second list.

Choosing the IPAM and DNS backends

Because Settings → DNS Records is a registry of N backends (§26.9), the wizard offers two selectors — IPAM backend (the address) and DNS backend (the hostname) — each listing only the enabled rows that carry that role.

  • Both default to Auto, which follows the scopes declared in Settings → DNS Records. Auto is byte-for-byte the behaviour of an install that never picks anything, which is what makes the selectors purely additive.
  • Every option prints the backend's provider and its declared scope (any (catch-all) when it declares none), because a name is not what decides which backend answers. The note under each selector repeats the scope of the current choice and the outcome of its last connection test.
  • A selector with no eligible row is disabled and says so, pointing at Settings → DNS Records.

A pick is validated, not trusted. The row you name is checked against the same rules Auto uses — read from the same scope column, not re-derived — and each way it can fail has its own code, because each has a different fix:

Code Meaning Fix
backend_unknown No such row (it was deleted since the page loaded). Reload the page.
backend_disabled The row exists but is disabled. Enable it in Settings.
backend_wrong_role The row does not carry the role you are using it for. Give it the role, or pick another row.
backend_out_of_scope The row's scope does not claim this zone or pool. Widen that backend's scope, or pick the one that claims it.

An invalid pick is refused, never quietly downgraded to Auto — even when a catch-all backend is present that would have answered. A silent fallback would run the work on a backend nobody named while the page still showed the one that was chosen.

A pick overrides the scope choice only; it never widens a scope. The scope is an earlier declaration by the same operator, and the wizard is not the place to overrule it by accident. What a pick does resolve is an AMBIGUOUS tie: both tied backends are in scope, so naming one is a legitimate answer to a question the configuration left open. That is the selectors' main use case.

Pick-level and scope-level blockers are kept apart. ipam_backend_rejected / dns_backend_rejected mean the backend you named cannot do this, and send you to that row. ipam_not_resolved / dns_not_resolved mean the scope rules produced no single answer, and send you to the scope rules. Folding them would send an operator who named a backend off to fix a scope, when the fix is to one row — or to the choice itself.

A chosen backend that cannot act raises a warning, not silence. Choosing an IPAM backend with Reserve the VIP from IPAM switched off, or a DNS backend with no hostname given, warns that nothing will be reserved or published. A control that silently does nothing reads as a control that worked.

Apply writes where Preview said it would. The plan records the backend ids it resolved, and Apply acts on those ids rather than resolving a second time. The registry is editable between the two presses, so a second resolution could answer differently and write to a backend the summary never named. A recorded null therefore means exactly one thing: no backend carried that role when the plan was built.

6. Cloning & migrating policies

Clone, Clone to and Migrate to recreate a whole policy tree (virtual server, VIP, pool + members, health checks, content routing, and optionally the full WAF profile) on the same or another FortiWeb. Migrate to clones first and disables the source only if the clone lands cleanly; the source is kept, never deleted.

Where to start:

  • One policy — on the Server Policy list (§5), select the row and press Clone, Clone to or Migrate to. The dialog opens on the list with that policy filled in.
  • Many policies — tick their checkboxes on the same list and press the same buttons: one dialog, one bulk run (§6.5). Clone to and Migrate to are disabled while no other FortiWeb is registered.

What the guided dialog does for you:

  • Pre-flight checklist (runs automatically): source readable, destination reachable, name collisions, WAF profile present/identical/different on the destination, VIP IP conflicts, certificate warnings (key material can only move over SSH), and capacity headroom. Blocking findings disable Apply.
  • Dummy VIP rules: cloned VIPs are rewritten to a placeholder IP so a clone can never take real traffic by accident. Admins configure the rewrite rules in Settings → Clone / Migrate. A rule replaces the leading octets and keeps the rest (198.51 → 240.51 turns 198.51.100.7 into 240.51.100.7); when no rule matches, the fallback address is used (default 203.0.113.9). Single clones can override the suggested IP; bulk clones always use the rules.
  • Admin defaults: whether the Web Protection Profile is copied by default comes from the same settings page and is shown read-only. Tick Override admin defaults to change it for this run only.
  • WAF profile choice: if the destination already has a different profile with the same name, you choose — use the destination's, or copy the source profile under a new name.
  • Objects that already exist on the destination are validated and skipped, never overwritten. The clone lands disabled for a manual cutover.
  • Rule content travels with the rule. Objects whose meaning lives in per-rule sub-tables — a Custom Access Rule's URL / source-IP / rate-limit filters, a URL Access Rule's match conditions — are copied with those rows, not as a bare name. A rule copied without them would appear on the destination and match no traffic, and nothing in the job result would say so. If a sub-table does not exist on the destination's firmware it contributes nothing rather than being invented.

6.1 Choosing what happens to the Web Protection Profile

A policy's WAF profile is the biggest thing a clone can bring with it, so it is the one decision the dialog always asks about. There are three answers:

Choice What lands on the destination
Copy the profile subtree the profile and all of its sub-tables are recreated. The default for a destination that does not have the profile.
Create it only if it is missing an existing profile with that name is left completely alone — object and sub-tables.
New, compare and decide you are shown every change this run would make inside the existing profile, and you tick the ones you want.

⚠ "Leave the subtree on" is not the same as "only if it is missing". With the subtree on, an existing profile object is left alone but its ~40 sub-tables are still classified one at a time — so a signature list the destination profile lacks gets added to a live, possibly shared, profile. If that is not what you want, pick only if it is missing.

Reuse a profile the destination already owns. Instead of copying anything, you can point the cloned policy at a profile that is already on the destination. The subtree is pruned and the policy's profile field is rewritten — pruning alone would leave the copy naming the source's profile, which the appliance answers with -651.

6.2 New, compare and decide — and what a "no" actually does

This is the only clone mode that edits a live object on purpose, so nothing is ever pre-ticked and the pre-flight says WARN, never ok.

You are shown two kinds of offer:

  • the profile's own fields that differ from the destination's ("retune"), each listed as field: destination -> source;
  • each row the run would add or change inside the profile's sub-tables.

Every box you leave unticked is a "keep the destination's own", and since 1.12.0 that answer is carried through completely:

  1. the declined item is removed from the plan, not skipped at write time — an item left in saying create describes a write that will not happen, and every count, report and verification reads the plan;
  2. every field still being written that NAMED the declined section is put back to the destination's own value. This is the half that used to be missing. Without it the profile was still written carrying the source's name for a section that was not being created, the destination ended up naming something it does not have, and the appliance seated a default of its own — so a "keep the original" produced neither the original nor the source;
  3. anything that was itself going to be created and can no longer stand — an object naming the declined section, or a row whose parent object you declined — is dropped too, transitively, and listed in the result under cascaded with the reason. It is never written and never silently blanked.

The run report names all three outcomes, so you can check the answer you gave against what the run actually did:

  • reverted — label · field · the destination value that was kept
  • cascaded — label · why it could no longer be created
  • dropped / kept / retuned — the counts

If the source changes between comparing and applying, the apply refuses. The comparison and the apply are two requests, and the apply re-plans. Offers are matched by a stable key built from what identifies the object on the appliance — collection, key, parent, kind — never by position. If the new plan offers something your answer never covered, SATOM stops and asks you to re-run the comparison. "Never shown, so skip it" would write nothing you saw and call the run green; "never shown, so take it" would write something you never saw at all.

6.3 Certificates, SNI and backends

  • SNI policies are cloned. The policy and its member rows travel over REST; no key material is involved (an SNI row names a certificate, it does not contain one).
  • Certificate key material can be carried over SSH, as part of the clone, when you enable it. It is fetched before the first write, because a certificate is a dependency: a failure halfway through an apply would leave you committed — on a migrate, after the source has already been disabled. A failure here blocks and writes nothing. A certificate name the destination already holds is left alone: overwriting one that is already serving traffic is a change to live traffic that nobody asked for. A certificate read without its private key cannot be carried — copying the public half alone would create a certificate the destination can never serve with.
  • Backend reachability (optional, off by default). Two independent checks that are never merged into one verdict: the destination appliance pings the backend itself, and this node opens a TCP connection to the real port. unknown is reported as unknown — it is not folded into either answer. It is off by default because a bulk run means one timeout per policy per member, and because it sends traffic to third-party hosts.

6.4 Rows the destination already owns

The appliance enforces uniqueness on a natural key — a subset of a row, not the whole row. So a destination row with the same key but different content used to be invisible to the planner and present to the box: the plan said create, the appliance refused the duplicate, and the destination went on serving the old value under a green run.

Such a row is now planned as update and written as the minimum edit — the destination's row with the source's non-empty fields laid over it, addressed by the destination's row id. A blank on the source means "this box does not use this field", not "erase what the other box has".

Consequence, stated plainly: a reconciled row is not a byte-for-byte copy of the source row. It is the destination's row carrying everything the source names. A row that must match exactly has to be deleted and re-created, and the cloner never deletes.

Turning reconciliation off does not silently skip those rows — it refuses the apply. A skipped row leaves the destination serving the old value under a run that looked successful.

6.5 Bulk runs

Bulk and the single-policy dialog go through the same function, so every option described above is true of a 60-policy run and of one dialog.

  • Profiles are handled once per run, keyed on the pair (source profile, landing profile). Two policies landing on the same profile name from different source profiles are not a repetition, and skipping the second would drop rows in silence.
  • Pre-flight analysis runs in parallel. Measured on a live appliance: 10 policies, 51.45 s → 20.99 s at 4 workers, with an identical plan footprint and the selection order preserved. The worker count is yours to set; the ceiling exists because the appliance saturates.

7. Server Objects & the generic object editor

Object pages are drawn from the device's own menu. In the FortiWeb ADOM the sidebar group FortiWeb lists every page SATOM has a measured GUI layout for on the selected device's firmware build, in FortiWeb's menu order (Server Objects → Server → Server Pool, System → Admin → Settings, and so on), and All pages shows the same menu as a grid. The layouts come with the knowledge packs, so the menu follows the build the device actually runs.

  • SATOM's old menus (Loadbalancer / Server Objects, WAF, Configuration) are no longer drawn. Old URLs and bookmarks redirect to the page of the device's menu that draws the same collection.
  • Not in GUI, but in CLI — a menu group of its own: every object the device's build has that no page of its GUI edits (measured: the crawl opens every menu entry and records what each page reads), one page per CLI root, with list, edit dialog and the usual dry run. Each page says so above its list. FortiADC has the same group (§17.1).
  • A page that the GUI draws with a widget SATOM cannot measure (Feature Visibility, Fabric Connectors, External Connector) is drawn from the build's CLI tree at its place in the menu.
  • A collection that no measured page draws yet has no menu entry. It comes back when its page is crawled.
  • FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator pages are built the same way and behave as described here, with one difference: their editors read the values from the device, where FortiWeb's read the SATOM cache.

Server Pool on fwb-01: FortiWeb's toolbar and columns inside the SATOM frame.

Working with a list page

  • Rows come from the SATOM cache. The badge at the right of the toolbar says when the cache was taken; ⟳ (Refresh) pulls the device's configuration into the cache and returns to the page (config_write). FortiWeb's predefined entries are read live from the device instead, carry a live badge and are read-only.
  • Click selects a row; double-click, Enter or Edit opens it in its editor. Search filters the rows.
  • Create New is FortiWeb's own menu. Where FortiWeb's layout has no Create New but SATOM's classic page had one (CA Group, CRL, admin replacement messages), a Create New button opens SATOM's object editor instead. It is never offered for certificates REST cannot create or for file-backed objects.
  • Clone copies the selected object under a new name, with its sub-table rows. Delete removes it. Both show a dry run first, and Delete runs the reference check in §7.2.
  • Save as template reads the selected object from the device and saves it to the Template Library as a pending template (§29), filed under the same section the classic page used. A Web Protection Profile is captured with its sub-policies. This needs the template-save permission.
  • Deep clone (inline Web Protection Profiles) copies the profile and the objects it references under new names. The Web Protection Profile list also has Hide default profiles and Factory catalog (§8).
  • Certificates: Import writes Local, CA, Intermediate CA and XML certificates over the certificate-only SSH session, because REST cannot create them. On Local certificates, Generate opens the Certificate Manager (§10).
  • File-backed objects (XML schema, WSDL, DTD, JSON schema, OpenAPI): Upload files the document in SATOM's artifact store, and Stored copies lists what is there.
  • Under the table, the config template library of the object's section lists the templates for this object type: View, Apply to devices (with dry-run preview and the compatibility verdict), Clone, Delete, New template.

The editor

Opening an object shows the dialog FortiWeb opens for it: its sections, tabs, folding blocks and inline tables, laid out for the device's build. §7.4 explains the banner and the badges, and §7.5 explains how Save works.

  • Inline tables (pool members, VIP lists, match conditions…) behave like FortiWeb's grid. A row opens in its own dialog. Create New is offered only for tables SATOM knows and can read, so a table SATOM cannot read is never written blind.
  • Reference selectors are filled from the device's own objects. The pencil beside one opens the selected object in a panel stacked over the dialog, the way FortiWeb drops in a sub-page. Esc closes the panel, and choices made in the panel feed back into the selector that opened it.
  • Below the main dialog, Not in GUI, but in CLI lists the fields this object has on the build that FortiWeb's GUI does not show (§7.6).

The stacked panel, and the Create New button that FortiWeb lacks, use SATOM's own object editor (objedit):

  • Fields render like the FortiWeb GUI: curated labels, enums with GUI names, toggles, reference dropdowns; anything uncurated still shows with a raw-JSON escape hatch, so nothing is uneditable.
  • Sub-tables are edited in place, several levels deep. Every reference dropdown has ✎ (edit the selected object) and ＋ (create a new one in place).
  • If the device is unreachable, the editor renders from the local cache with an info banner. Fields stay editable and Save still targets the device.
  • Every save previews as a dry-run diff before applying.

7.1 Reference fields are checked before the write

A reference field does not take free text: it names an object that must already exist on the appliance (a URL-rewrite policy, a user-tracking policy, a certificate…). If you save a name the device does not have, FortiWeb refuses the whole save with errcode -651: Invalid input value. — a message that names neither the field nor the value, and that also discards the correct fields you changed in the same save.

SATOM asks the appliance first. When a value is not there you get a refusal that says which field, which value, which collection, and which names do exist:

subresource-integrity-policy: "admin" — "waf/subresource-integrity-policy" has no configured objects on this device, so there is nothing "subresource-integrity-policy" can name yet

Three things worth knowing:

  • The check runs on Preview as well as on Apply. A preview that hid a certain refusal would have you approve a plan the device will reject.
  • Nothing is written when a reference is refused — not even the fields that were fine. Fix the value and save again.
  • If the appliance cannot be reached for the check, the save is not blocked. The response lists the fields it could not verify (unverified_refs); the device remains the authority and will still answer -651 if the value is wrong.

A field that offers a dropdown is a reference field. A few fields that the appliance treats as selects still render as text because the collection they draw from could not be confirmed on this firmware — those are passed to the device unchecked, exactly as before.

7.2 Deleting an object that something else uses

Delete refuses while another object still names the one you are removing. The appliance keeps its own count of references, and SATOM reads it before sending anything:

refusing to delete "urw-full": it is referenced by 2 object(s) — inline-protection(wpp-full-lab), inline-protection(wpp-pol-shop-cms). Remove those references first, then delete it.

Why this exists: FortiWeb does not reliably refuse deleting an object that is in use. When it accepts one, nothing fails — the profiles and policies that named it keep pointing at a name that no longer resolves, and you find out when traffic breaks.

What to expect:

  • The check runs on the pre-check, before the confirmation prompt. You see the refusal instead of confirming a delete that should not happen.
  • Some collections report how many references there are but not which. The message says so rather than showing an empty list.
  • If the object cannot be read back from the appliance, it is not deleted — there is no way to tell an unreferenced object from an unreadable one.
  • If this firmware does not report a reference count for that collection at all, the delete proceeds as before. A capability the device lacks is not treated as a refusal.
  • Deleting a row inside an object (a sub-table entry) is not affected: the parent's reference count says nothing about one of its rows.

To remove an object that is genuinely referenced, clear the references first — the message names where to look. If you are certain the appliance's count is wrong, the delete endpoint accepts force: true; forced deletes are recorded in the audit log as ref_check=forced.

7.3 Fields the build does not have, and fields only the CLI serves

Every Save is also checked against the appliance's exact firmware build (see Build compatibility). The preview shows the result above the request, in a yellow box (red when it blocks):

  • Applies, but on 8.0.6 token-secret does not exist in …: it will be skipped — the field is removed from the write instead of being sent and silently dropped by the appliance (FortiWeb answers 200 for a field it does not have). When SATOM knows the new name it says so in brackets. If every field you changed is missing on that build, the save is refused.
  • … = '…' is not valid in … (allowed: …): blocked or … is out of range …: blocked — a value the build does not accept. The Apply is refused (Refused by the build compatibility check: …); the dry run still shows it.
  • not measured on X — cannot be guaranteed — SATOM has no evidence for that build. The write goes ahead; harvest the build (§30.12) to know.

On some builds some settings exist only in the CLI. For those fields the editor uses the CLI writer (CLI writer):

  1. Preview. Below the REST request a card CLI script — fields this build serves only by CLI shows exactly what will be typed (config / edit / set / next / end; secrets masked). A dialect not yet verified on a lab box is labelled dialect not lab-verified.
  2. Apply. REST is sent first; the CLI script runs only if REST succeeded. If the appliance rejects a line, the change is discarded with abort — nothing half-applied — and the card says CLI refused: … and whether the readback confirms nothing was applied.
  3. Readback. After the CLI script, SATOM reads the object back in a new session (and over REST when REST serves it) and shows Readback (CLI) and Readback (REST), field by field. The editor does not reload, so the readback stays on screen. A field that reads back different fails the save and is named.

Today this rarely shows: FortiWeb 7.6.8 and 8.0.6 have no CLI-only field, so every FortiWeb field still goes by REST. Fields SATOM cannot classify on the build are listed as Not known on this build (sent by REST as before). The permission is unchanged (the editor's write permission); every CLI write is in the audit log as config.cli_write, with field names and the outcome, never a value.

The cards above belong to SATOM's object editor (the stacked panel and the SATOM editor pages). On a page in the device's layout the same split runs on the server, and the Server Policy dialog marks such a field CLI in the Channel column of its review (§7.5).

On FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator pages in the device's layout, the "Not in GUI, but in CLI" section is part of the form, as on FortiWeb (§7.6). On the FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer tabs, the section is itself the editor of those fields (Read values over CLI, Preview CLI change, Apply). Objects only the CLI serves are edited the same way on the device's Not in GUI, but in CLI page (§7.7). On FortiAuthenticator they are also edited on the menu page that hosts them, which says Served only by the CLI on this build.

7.4 Pages in FortiWeb's layout: banner and badges

The note above every list and dialog names the layout it is drawn from: FortiWeb 7.6.x GUI layout — template built from FortiWeb 7.6.8 build …. This device runs 7.6.8. A knowledge pack badge means the layout came from an imported knowledge pack. Hover the badge to see where it came from. When the fit is not exact, the note becomes a warning:

Banner Meaning
No layout was measured on … itself; this one is from …, the closest build of the same train Fields this device has and the layout does not place are listed under Not in GUI, but in CLI (§7.6).
This layout was built from … Newer firmware adds or renames fields … The device runs a newer build than any layout. Fields the newer build adds are not shown in the form.
… older than every layout template … Some fields shown may not exist on this firmware The device runs an older build than any layout.
The firmware of this device is not known yet Run a firmware check on the device.
Operation mode not cached for this device Fields that depend on the operation mode are shown and marked.

Fields show and hide as you edit, the way FortiWeb's GUI does: every field and section carries FortiWeb's condition, and the device's facts are already applied. A condition SATOM cannot evaluate leaves the field shown. When FortiWeb would hide fields for the current values, the title bar says N fields hidden by FortiWeb for these settings.

Badges next to a label:

Badge Meaning
conditional FortiWeb shows this field only under a condition SATOM cannot evaluate here. Hover to see what it depends on.
key not measured The GUI crawl could not tell which REST field this control shows. Hover to see the candidates.
choices not measured FortiWeb offers a list of choices the crawl could not read. Type the value the way the CLI takes it.
No API on this build (GUI only) The field has no API on this build. It is shown the way the GUI shows it and is never saved. A whole page can be GUI-only too, and is then drawn read-only.
read-only / an endpoint name FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator: the GUI draws the field read-only, or saves it into another object that is edited on its own page.

Edit Address on fgt-01: conditional fields and "choices not measured" badges.

A settings page (a single object such as System → Admin → Settings) adds Save as template, which captures the whole object as a pending template, and ⟳, which refreshes it from the device, to the page header. The section's config template library is listed below the form.

7.5 How a save travels

The same sequence runs on every page in a device's layout. Nothing is written before you have seen the change.

  1. Save collects the fields you changed. Fields hidden by the show/hide rules are not sent, and a field you did not touch is never sent back. Changed fields in Not in GUI, but in CLI travel with the rest.
  2. SATOM runs a dry run for each object the change touches. Most changes touch only the dialog's own object. A field that FortiWeb's GUI saves into another object goes to that object, and a form that FortiWeb's GUI writes through its own GUI API goes through that API.
  3. Review the change lists each field with Was, New and Channel (REST, REST (GUI API) or CLI). An Endpoint column appears when more than one object is involved, and the raw request is folded underneath. Choose Back to the form or Apply to .
  4. Apply writes the objects in order and stops at the first refusal. The message names the endpoint that refused and what was already written.
  5. On FortiWeb object pages and in the Server Policy dialog, the server checks the change before anything leaves SATOM, in this order: - a template-managed Web Protection Profile is read-only: the save is refused and points you to the Template Library. This holds when the profile is opened from a policy's pencil, too; - another user's edit lease on the object blocks the save, and nothing is sent. A row of an inline table is checked against its parent's lease; - every reference value must exist on the device (§7.1); - the build compatibility check runs (§7.3): a blocking finding refuses the apply and names the finding, and fields the build does not have are stripped instead of being lost behind a success. The dry run is never refused by this check; the object editor shows its report in the review. If every changed field is missing on the build, nothing is saved.

The channels then split. REST fields go by REST. Fields the build serves only by CLI go through the CLI writer over SSH, and only after the REST part succeeded. If REST fails, the CLI part is not sent. The Channel column of the review names the CLI fields of every object in the change, a bound object's included. 6. After a successful apply, SATOM releases your edit lease on the object (a row of an inline table leaves its parent's lease alone), updates its copy and the page reloads. FortiGate and FortiAuthenticator pages re-read the object from the device. If the device stored a different value, the page says Saved, but the device stored different values: ….

System → Admin → Settings on fwb-01, with "Not in GUI, but in CLI" below the form.

7.6 Not in GUI, but in CLI

Every object editor, for all five products, ends with a collapsed section titled Not in GUI, but in CLI (n). SATOM shows every field the device has on its exact build. A field the Fortinet GUI does not show is never dropped and never merged into another group: it goes here. The section is always drawn, even when it is empty. An empty section says why: every field is in the GUI, or the page's GUI layout has not been measured yet.

Two kinds of evidence decide what is "not in the GUI":

  • the API library of the device's exact build: a field the CLI has and REST does not is never in the GUI;
  • the page's GUI layout, where one was measured: a REST field the layout does not place is not in the GUI either. Without a measured layout SATOM cannot tell a GUI field from a REST-only one, so those stay in their usual groups and the section says so.

Each field carries the channel SATOM writes it by:

Badge Meaning
REST The REST API serves it. A normal Save writes it.
CLI This build does not serve it over REST. Save writes it over SSH through the CLI writer.
unverified on this build No source measured the field on this build. It is shown, never hidden. It is not written until a channel is measured.

Edit Server Pool on fwb-01: the member table and the collapsed "Not in GUI, but in CLI (7)" section.

In an editor you can write to, the fields in the section are part of the form, and Save sends them with the rest (§7.5). On a Create New form, a CLI-only field says set it once the object exists.

Read values over CLI appears when the section has CLI fields and the object exists. It reads their current values over a read-only SSH session (show full-configuration) and fills them into the inputs; a value you leave unchanged is not sent back. Secrets are never returned: their input says secret — not shown. Reading needs only view permission. Nothing is written.

Where a view has no editor of its own (the FortiADC and FortiAnalyzer tabs, objects only the CLI serves, read-only users), the section is a table of Field / Channel / Type / Value:

  • With config_write, each CLI field is an input. Name the row (and its parent row, for a nested table), then use Read values over CLI, Preview CLI change, which shows the script, and Apply.
  • REST fields show written by the object's own form.
  • Unverified fields show not writable until measured on this build.
  • A write that names any REST or unmeasured field is refused whole (nothing was sent: …), so a half-applied change cannot happen.
  • When the product's CLI dialect has not been verified on a device yet, a note asks you to read the previewed script before you apply.
  • Every apply is recorded in the audit log as appliance.not_in_gui.save.

7.7 The per-device page

Appliances → device → Not in GUI, but in CLI (/appliances/<id>/not-in-gui) lists everything the device's build has outside the Fortinet GUI, in one place. Every section in the views links to it as Everything this device has outside the GUI →. The same inventory is on the console, without the values and the editor: sudo satom get device not-in-gui <device> [--endpoint <key>].

The per-device page for fwb-01: layout-measured pages, CLI-only objects and CLI-only fields.

  • Layout-measured pages: for each page whose GUI layout was measured, the REST fields the Fortinet GUI does not show.
  • Objects the device's GUI does not draw: whole objects the device serves over REST that no page of its own GUI reads on this build (FortiADC 7.6.7: VDOM and VDOM links, per-VDOM syslog and FortiAnalyzer, DNS, ISP provinces, connection pool, alert targets…), each with its rows, read from the device when the page opens (read only; secrets are never shown) and a link to the page SATOM draws it on. On FortiADC the list also names what the build serves that no measured page reads at all (7.6.7: Auto Backup, whose GUI tab is an action): this page is where SATOM shows it. An object the build answers 404 for is not listed.
  • Objects only the CLI serves: whole objects REST does not have at all (for example FortiAuthenticator system/dns). Each one is editable as described in §7.6.
  • CLI-only fields of objects the REST API serves: per object, editable the same way.

If the device's running build is unknown, the page asks you to run a firmware check first. For a product with no measured GUI layout and no measured CLI tree, the page says that SATOM cannot split GUI fields from CLI-only fields yet. In that case every field the REST API returns stays in the object views, and nothing is hidden.

8. Web Protection (WAF)

In the FortiWeb ADOM, the Web Protection pages belong to the device's own menu: the FortiWeb group in the sidebar. SATOM builds that group from the measured GUI layout of the selected device's firmware build (the layouts come with the knowledge packs). The pages therefore have the same names and sit in the same places as in that FortiWeb's GUI. Web Protection Profile is under Policy (Inline / Offline tabs). The protection areas are under Web Protection. On a 7.6 build these are Known Attacks (Signatures / Custom Signature), Protocol, Access, Input Validation, Cookie Security, Advanced Protection and Data Loss Prevention. Another build shows whatever its own GUI has. All pages at the top of the group lists every page in the device's menu order.

The old SATOM WAF group of the FortiWeb ADOM (Web Protection Profile, Web Protection and the protection areas) is gone. Its links still work: an old URL redirects to the device-menu page that draws the same collection. With no device selected, or no measured layout for it yet, the FortiWeb group shows only Server Policy. A collection that no measured page draws yet has no menu entry until its page is crawled. The fleet-wide WAF pages and the device-scoped WAF tools (Search Attack ID, Exceptions & Signature, WAF Artifacts) are under Operations → WAF (§13.1, §13.2).

8.1 Web Protection Profiles and signatures in the device menu

Web Protection Profile is a FortiWeb-layout list, with the SATOM tools the old profile page had:

  • Deep clone (Inline tab) copies the profile and the objects it references (sub-policies, signatures, rules) under new names.
  • Save as template reads the selected profile from the device and saves it to the Template Library as a pending template.
  • Hide default profiles hides the predefined profiles. It is a per-user preference, the same one the old page used.
  • Factory catalog opens the predefined profiles per firmware build and API version.
  • A template-managed profile carries a Template badge. On this device it is read-only: Edit becomes View, and Delete is unavailable. To change it, edit it in the Template Library.

The Web Protection Profile list in FortiWeb's own layout, with SATOM's profile tools

Known Attacks → Signatures is a FortiWeb-layout list as well. Each signature policy opens in the FortiWeb-layout object editor.

Known Attacks → Signatures, drawn from the device's own GUI layout

SATOM's own tools are still served:

  • Signatures editor: browse signature categories, search the full signature catalog (2,400+ signatures by name/class/state), open any signature's details, disable it, set alert-only, or add a per-signature exception, with the same element-type-gated form as the appliance GUI. No menu entry leads to it on a device whose layout draws the Signatures page. Open it at /web/web-protection/<device id>/signatures/<signature policy>.
  • 166 curated object kinds (ported from the desktop manager and validated against the vendor admin guide) drive SATOM's own object forms: correct enums, field gating, inline help ("what does this do", "how the backend reacts"), and an explanation under every Action dropdown.
  • Regex Lab: open it from the Tools menu in the top bar (Regex calculator, Regex cheat sheet, Pattern library) on any page. In SATOM's own object editor, in the dialogs of the pages in FortiWeb's layout (the Server Policy dialog included) and on the Exceptions page, every regex-capable field also has a .* button. That button opens the lab on the field and writes the tested pattern back into it. The lab tests patterns server-side with curated examples per section. Its rewrite preview numbers captures the way FortiWeb and FortiADC do: $0 is the first ( … ) group, $1 the second.
  • In SATOM's own editor, profile-level editing shows each sub-policy as a dropdown with Edit/＋, down to six levels of nesting.

8.2 Signature source, signature index and database freshness

Every FortiWeb downloads its own signature database from FortiGuard. SATOM does not ship signatures, and new signatures need no SATOM release or pack. SATOM reads them off a device instead.

The signature source. On Administrator → Signatures, choose one FortiWeb as the signature source: one with a valid FortiGuard licence that updates on schedule. Save and collect now reads its whole signature catalog right away. This runs as a background job, which the job dock tracks. The read is REST and read-only:

What How
Database versions GET /api/v2.0/system/config.fortiguard returns, in one call, the attack-signature DB and the other databases the firmware reports (antivirus, IP reputation, GeoIP, known bots…), with their last update and licence validity. The fallback is diagnose system update info over SSH (signature DB only).
Catalog waf/signature.advanced.dictionaries + .details: every main class, sub-class and signature with its description

The signature index. SATOM indexes each read locally: every signature id with its class, description and lineage (the DB version it first appeared in, last seen, removed in). It also keeps a snapshot per database version.

  • A read whose content equals the latest snapshot writes nothing.
  • A new version records what it added, changed (description or class) and removed, and notifies every administrator in the in-app bell. The snapshot history lists it, with a details page.
  • The first snapshot is the baseline: its signatures are not reported as new.
  • A read that returns no signatures is refused, so it never empties the index.

The page searches the index by id, description or class (removed signatures on request). The index also rewrites the catalog that the signature editor and the WPP views read. The signature_sync scheduled action collects too, but only from the configured source. It refuses any other target, so another box's older database can never appear as a fleet change.

Freshness, every FortiWeb. The daily scheduled action signature_check reads the database versions of every FortiWeb (one REST call per box) and records when they last changed. When the source's signature version is not the one the index holds, it collects and indexes the catalog in the same round. A failed catalog read makes the round red.

The page lists every device with:

  • its signature DB version and the channel it came from (rest or cli);
  • last update and licence;
  • the other databases;
  • the time of the check;
  • a status: current, stale or unreadable.

The alert engine (§26.6) raises a device alert in any of these cases:

  • The device's signature database is older than 7 days. Age is measured from the device's own "last update" time. When the device gives none, it is measured from when SATOM saw the version change.
  • The device reports that it never downloaded an update. When the device reports an invalid FortiGuard licence, the alert names it as the reason.
  • The device's version cannot be read: REST and SSH both refused.

These alerts share the family, toggle, routing and cooldown of the other device-health alerts. The limit is the setting alerts.signature_max_days.

FortiWebs registered with no signature source, or with a source that no longer exists, raise device.signature_source_missing. Devices in maintenance are skipped. A node updated from 2.x has no signature_check row until you create it (sudo satom execute seed actions --yes on the primary, §22.4).

A knowledge pack can carry signature metadata: public FortiGuard encyclopedia data (name, severity, category, CVEs, a link). None does yet, because FortiGuard's terms do not permit redistributing it, so the section ships empty until they do. When a pack carries it, the signature search shows a severity badge and the CVEs next to each id it knows, and the signature's details add a FortiGuard row. Ids with no metadata show as before.

9. Exceptions & signature carve-outs

Exceptions & Signature is the single place to author every policy-bound carve-out (WAF exceptions and signature customizations) for one FortiWeb. It is in the Operations → WAF submenu of the FortiWeb ADOM, next to Search Attack ID and WAF Artifacts. It is not on the Global console's WAF menu, because it is a FortiWeb-ADOM page and a link from Global would switch the tab's ADOM. The URL is /web/exceptions/<device id>.

The page always works on one device: the one selected in the FortiWeb ADOM (§3.1). Pick it on the Service Diagram or with change next to the device name at the top of the sidebar. If no device is selected, /web/exceptions/ sends you to the Service Diagram to pick one.

The page title names the device: Exceptions & Signature Carve-outs — . The carve-outs it lists are desired state recorded in SATOM. Authoring writes nothing to the box: pushing is a separate step. To see who across the estate holds a given carve-out, use Fleet inventory at the top of the page. It opens Operations → WAF → Exceptions (§13.1).

Operations → WAF → Exceptions & Signature: the carve-outs authored for fwb-01

The team rules the app enforces:

  1. Templates stay clean. A template-managed WAF profile cannot receive exceptions — the app blocks the save and offers the fix.
  2. Guided clone. When you try to except a locked/shared profile, the app proposes cloning it for that specific server policy (name suggested by the Naming catalog), re-binds the policy to the clone, moves the carve-outs, and re-submits your change — one flow.
  3. Lifecycle. Exceptions are bound to server policies. Deleting a policy purges its carve-outs; swapping a policy's WAF profile flags them STALE (never silently deleted) with a banner to re-target. A change made on the device itself, outside SATOM, is caught when the page opens: such carve-outs are flagged DRIFT (below).
  4. Capacity. Injections check device limits (e.g. 128 filter entries per signature set) and clone operations check profile headroom.

Other tools on the page:

  • ⬆ Inject to device — push authored exceptions onto the box: pick the live target object, review the dry-run plan, apply.
  • 🔎 Detect on device — read the exceptions that already exist on a box and import them as desired-state, bound to the right policy.
  • Which Server Policy holds a carve-out: a count of carve-outs per Server Policy, unbound ones included. A banner above it names the carve-outs that went stale because their Server Policy was re-bound to another profile. Edit a stale carve-out to re-point it (saving clears the flag), or delete it.
  • DRIFT — not on the device: each time the page opens, SATOM reads the device's Server Policies and the profile each one uses, and compares them with the carve-outs. A carve-out is flagged DRIFT when no Server Policy it names is still on the device using the profile it was authored for: the policy is gone, or it now uses another Web Protection Profile. That happens when the change was made on the device itself, outside SATOM, where the re-bind hooks behind STALE never ran. A warning banner gives the count, n carve-out(s) no longer match the device, with Show them; each such row carries a DRIFT warning badge next to its category; and the State filter has a not on the device option. Re-point each one at the policy's current profile, or delete it. Carve-outs already flagged STALE and carve-outs bound to no policy are never flagged DRIFT. If the device's policy list cannot be read, nothing is flagged: an unreachable device is not evidence that a policy is gone.
  • Filters (type, category, Server Policy, state, free text over name, profile, policy and payload) are applied by the server, so the counts match the rows you see.
  • Per carve-out: Inject (push to this device), Deploy (place it on other FortiWebs), Versions and rollback, and Delete. A rollback adds a new version and deletes nothing. Deleted carve-outs that can still be brought back are listed separately, with their bindings.
  • Analyse before implementing — SATOM's own deterministic analysis of the draft is available to anyone who can open the page; the assistant's opinion (the draft is sent to the configured AI provider) is added only for users holding advisor.use.

Authoring, injecting, deploying, deleting and detecting need config_write; without it the page is read-only and those buttons are hidden or disabled. Deleting always goes through the impact check (the guarded delete).

9.1 Search Attack ID — from a block page to a reviewed carve-out

When FortiWeb blocks a request it shows the caller a block page carrying an Attack ID (000000004106). That number is the only thing the person who was blocked can give you, and on its own it says nothing. Search Attack ID resolves it. Paste the reference from the block page and SATOM finds the attack-log entry it refers to. The whole triage is then on one page: what was blocked, why, whether it should have been, and the exception that would let it through if it should not.

Search Attack ID is in the Operations → WAF submenu of the FortiWeb ADOM (/waf/attack-search/). It does not depend on the device selected in the sidebar: the reference chooses the appliance.
