  • The full reference, id-<device>-<number> (for example id-fwb-01-000000004106), names the appliance. SATOM matches it against appliance names, ignoring case. If no name matches, SATOM tries management addresses and warns that the device may have been renamed since the block page was served.
  • A bare MSG ID (000000004106, or unpadded 4106) names no device. Pick the appliance yourself.
  • An appliance you pick explicitly always wins over the one in the reference.

Opening the page, searching, explaining a field and building a carve-out need only the view permission. Analyze and Ask the AI about this field need advisor.use. Saving a carve-out, accepting or rejecting a drafted one, and inserting it need config_write.

Operations → WAF → Search Attack ID in the FortiWeb ADOM

Everything on this page reads. Nothing is pushed to an appliance until you explicitly ask for it in §9.6, and no draft leaves the page approved.

The results table lists date, MSG ID, type, subtype, policy, source and destination address, and action. If the ID matches nothing — a stale block page, the log rotated, the wrong appliance — you get the most recent entries instead, in the same columns, so the page never answers with an empty box you cannot act on.

One extra column matters before you touch anything: the Web Protection Profile behind each policy, and whether it is shared. A profile that only this Server Policy binds takes an exception in one click. A profile that four sites share does not — see §9.5. The column names the other policies when it is shared, and reads unknown when SATOM could not read the bindings off the device, because "could not ask" and "binds nothing" are opposite facts.

9.2 The entry panel: explaining one element at a time

Click any row and a panel slides in from the right with the full entry — around twenty-two fields, each on its own line. Two icons sit beside every one:

  • ⓘ Explain this field. Opens a short local reading directly under the field: what the element is, what this value classifies as, and what to look at next. It is computed on this node from the value alone. There is no WHOIS, no geolocation and no threat-feed call — your client's addresses, hosts and URLs are not sent anywhere, and the page still works on an isolated management network. The single exception is a reverse-DNS lookup against this host's own resolver, hard-capped at 1.5 seconds.
  • 💬 Ask the AI about this field. Sends the question on the click and renders the Advisor's answer underneath that same explanation. Leave it there for a general reading, or type your own question in the box below and press Ctrl+Enter (⌘+Enter on a Mac); follow-ups continue the same thread, so a second question does not mean restating the entry. This icon is drawn only when Scout, the AI assistant, is enabled (§33) — a button that could only ever refuse teaches you to distrust the buttons.

This path explains and cannot author: it is told not to draft a carve-out, none is returned to the screen, and one drafted anyway is dismissed rather than left waiting as an unreviewed proposal.

Every analysis on the page — local or AI — is stamped with the same line: engine, elapsed time, and tokens. no tokens means it was computed locally and spent none; tokens not reported means the provider did not say, which is not the same claim as zero. Failures are stamped too: a provider that burned forty seconds and then failed still burned them.

9.3 Building the exception

Below the entry sits the carve-out builder. It opens with a proposed kind of exception and the scope already ticked, and tells you why for each box.

  • The kind is derived from what actually blocked the request. A block by HTTP Protocol Constraints is not fixed by a signature exception, and the log line does not say so in those words.
  • Required fields are always taken. FortiWeb keys an Allow Method or HTTP-constraint exception on a URL pattern; leaving it out produces no exception at all, so it is marked required up front rather than offered as an optional narrowing.
  • A signature exception takes exactly one element — the most precise the entry carries. FortiWeb matches one element per row, so ticking URL and source address cannot mean "both"; SATOM uses the more precise one and says which of your ticks it could not honour.
  • The source address is held back while the request can be described by URL or host. It identifies the caller, not the traffic, so an exception scoped to it stops applying the moment that integration is re-addressed. It is one click away and the reason it was left off is on screen.

Everything stays editable — this is a starting point, not a decision. Only fields that narrow are ever pre-ticked, so the default cannot widen a carve-out, and unticking immediately restores the explanation of what is now missing.

Preview assembles the payload on the server from the row the appliance returned, and shows you the route (policy → profile → module → type), the breadth — what stops being inspected and what still applies — and the exact body. Breadth is computed from the payload, not from the type: a signature exception is the narrowest thing there is only if it names an element.

9.4 Asking the AI to judge the entry

Analyze sends the entry to the Advisor and returns a verdict (false-positive, true-attack, or uncertain), a risk level, and — when it judges the block a false positive at low or medium risk — a drafted exception you can accept, adapt, or reject.

  • SATOM never sends the row your browser is holding. It sends which entry and which appliance, and re-reads the entry from the device. A browser that can supply the evidence can invent it.
  • Verdict and risk are read from the model's own declared lines. If they are missing they stay empty — "the model would not judge" and "the model judged it harmless" cannot look the same on a screen that authorises an exception.
  • If the model drafts a proposal that contradicts its own verdict, the page says so in red instead of offering an ordinary Accept.
  • Accept saves a draft. It does not push anything to the appliance.

The verdict advises; you authorise. You can author a carve-out the Advisor did not recommend — the common case is a real attack pattern that a known caller must be allowed to send — but contradicting the verdict (a true-attack reading, or a high/unacceptable risk) requires a written justification of at least twenty characters, stored on the rule and in the audit log. Refusing it outright would not prevent the exception; it would move it to the CLI, where nothing records why.

9.5 Shared and template profiles

An exception lives on the Web Protection Profile, and FortiWeb records nothing about which Server Policy it was authored for. So a carve-out on a profile that four sites share applies to all four.

SATOM reads the bindings off the device and resolves one of four states:

state what happens
exclusive — this policy owns the profile authored directly; no clone, because there is nothing to protect it from
shared — other policies bind it too refused, naming the other policies, with the guided clone offered
template-managed refused the same way (team rule 1, §9)
unknown — the device could not be read treated as shared. Unknown is never assumed safe

The guided clone derives a policy-specific profile, re-binds the Server Policy to it, and authorises the exception there. The clone is a real write to the appliance and is never implicit — it happens only when you ask for it in the same action.

The copy is deep. A profile is not one object: it names roughly forty sub-policies, and a carve-out physically lands inside one of them. A profile that shares its sub-policies therefore shares every carve-out written into them, and a clone that copied only the top object would look isolated while leaking exactly as before. So every sub-object the new profile may own is recreated under this policy's own name — am-shop becomes am-shop-pol-shop-cms — and the references are re-pointed to the copies.

Three things are not copied, and SATOM says so before it writes anything:

left shared why can you override it?
predefined objects (Standard Protection, Predefined - Known Bots…) a copy stops receiving FortiGuard updates yes, object by object
objects an approved template governs copying takes this policy out of the template without anyone deciding to yes, object by object
anything whose parent stays shared re-pointing a reference is a write to the parent, so the copy would push the new name into an object other profiles still read no — it is a consequence, not a choice

The Exceptions page previews the clone first: what will be copied, what will stay shared, and the reason for each. Applying a plan that leaves anything shared takes an explicit confirmation, because a profile that is isolated in most places is not a state you can reason about three months later.

Capacity is checked for the whole plan, per object type, before the first write — a clone that dies half-way is not re-bound, and its orphans have to be found by hand. Object types with no configured limit are listed as unchecked rather than passed over quietly.

Saving a draft on the Exceptions page (§9) warns rather than refuses: a draft in the database lets nothing through. The Attack ID page refuses, because it is one click from a push. The push itself refuses hardest — that is where the leak physically happens.

9.6 Putting the rule on the appliance

Insert is two steps on purpose. The first returns the exact method, endpoint and body SATOM would send, and writes nothing. The second sends it. Approving a rule and approving a specific POST against a production WAF are different acts. It uses the same planner as the Exceptions page.

9.7 What is recorded

Every search, every field question with its question text verbatim, every analysis, and every decision goes to the audit log. Accepting a proposal records both the payload the model proposed and the one you approved — those are different facts and an auditor needs both. Rejecting one is recorded too, not erased.

9.8 Every carve-out records the build it was written for

A FortiWeb answers a write carrying a field its build does not know with 200 and discards the field — so a carve-out authored on one build and pushed to another can land without the very field that made it a carve-out, and report success. Every carve-out (and its fleet library item) therefore records the firmware build and REST API version of the appliance it was authored on:

  • a copy placed on another appliance keeps the source build, because its payload was written against that build;
  • editing the payload restamps it; a rollback or restore brings back the build of the old payload. The stamp is versioned but kept out of the content hash, so no existing history gained a version;
  • Inject to device and the Attack ID insert check the payload against the target's running build with the template rules (§29.1.1): a field the build discarded, renamed or does not serve blocks the push. A user with Approve templates (operations.template_approve) can override with a reason, audited as exception.compat.override.

The API sweep does not measure the carve-out sub-tables yet, so most pushes show no evidence for their fields: that is a warning, never a pass, and the gate starts to bite on its own once a sweep or a knowledge pack records those fields. Line Profiles show the build of each line's WPP template and the builds its approval covers.

10. Certificate Manager

Automation → Certificate Manager — in the Global ADOM, and in every device ADOM under Operations › Automation (product-scoped: in the FortiWeb ADOM you see FortiWeb material, in ADC the ADC material, in Global both). SATOM manages certificates on FortiWeb and FortiADC only, so the FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs show the entry disabled with that reason, and Global's Scan devices skips those kinds instead of listing them as unreachable. Administrator role (user_manage) required.

  • Inventory & scan: sweeps each device's certificate stores (FortiWeb via REST/SSH, FortiADC via REST), parses X.509 (CN, SANs, issuer, validity) and maps bindings — which policies / SSL profiles / admin GUI actually use each certificate. Removal is fail-closed: a bound or unverifiable certificate is refused.
  • Issuance — three origins (New certificate, one tab each; the inventory also has Generate CSR and Import buttons that open the right tab):
  • Signed by the configured CA: SATOM creates the CSR and signs it through the configured protocol — Microsoft ADCS or ACME (Let's Encrypt-style, http-01/dns-01) — the protocol is a Settings dropdown, not a code change.
  • CSR for another CA: SATOM generates the key and the CSR. The key stays in SATOM, encrypted; the row waits as awaiting signature. Its page shows 1. Download the CSR (file or copy) and 2. Import the signed certificate (paste or upload the PEM; a chain after the leaf is fine). The import is refused unless the certificate's public key is the stored key and every requested SAN is present. A pasted private key or a PKCS#12 is refused there too: the request's key was made in SATOM and a PKCS#12 would bring another one.
  • Import certificate + key: for a certificate whose CSR was made outside SATOM — a PEM certificate and its key, or a PKCS#12 with its password. The key is stored encrypted and marked key from outside.
  • Rotation (renew → swap → off the device → out of SATOM). A renewal never replaces the certificate in place: it is issued and deployed under a new name N days before expiry, and takes over every binding of the old one N days later (its swap date). The old certificate stays on the device so Roll back can return the bindings in one click; it leaves the device N days after the swap, and its key leaves SATOM N days after that (serial, dates and timeline stay as the record). The four numbers are defaults in Settings → Certificate Manager → Lifecycle policy and can be set per certificate on its page; the swap delay has to be shorter than the renew window, so the swap lands before the old certificate expires. With Renew automatically on, the sweep does the renewal itself for the configured CA. For another CA it generates the new CSR and notifies you, and the swap is scheduled when you import the signed certificate. Imported certificates are only notified: renew them outside and use Replace. Swap now skips the wait.
  • Revoke works with whichever CA is configured: SATOM runs that CA's revoke command. When it cannot (no revoke command, or a certificate signed by another CA), the certificate is marked revoked and the revocation register keeps it pending at the CA until someone confirms it there. Every revocation is in the register (serial, fingerprint, reason, who, result), and the register outlives a deleted record. A certificate still in use is refused unless you tick "revoke even though it is in use" (a compromised key). With the rotation's "revoke the old certificate", the old one is revoked (reason superseded) as it leaves the device, never while it still serves.
  • Delete asks for confirmation and is refused while the certificate is bound, or when its bindings cannot be read. It can revoke first and take it off the device first; either failing stops the delete.
  • A CA in an OPNsense firewall (System › Trust) signs through the ADCS command template with the bundled signer scripts/opnsense_ca_signer.py. Set CA to https://<firewall>:<port>, CA name to the issuing CA's refid, User to an API key whose user has only the System: Certificate Manager privilege, and the API secret in the password box. The class template is the OPNsense certificate type (server_cert, usr_cert, combined_server_client). Submit command: /opt/satom/venv/bin/python /opt/satom/scripts/opnsense_ca_signer.py sign --url {ca} --ca-ref {ca_name} --key {user} --cert-type {template} --csr {csr} --out {out} --pin-sha256 <pin>. Get the pin with … opnsense_ca_signer.py pin --url https://<firewall>:<port> and compare it with the firewall's certificate before saving it. The signer checks the pin before it sends any credential. The private key stays in SATOM: OPNsense receives only the CSR. OPNsense's CSR signing drops the request's subjectAltName, so the signer sends the SANs separately. The signed certificate stays in the firewall's Trust store as the CA's issuance record.
  • The CA secret is also passed to the signer as $SATOM_CA_SECRET, so a submit or revoke command can leave out {password} and keep the secret off the command line. {password} still works for signers that only take it there (certipy).
  • Deploy: FortiWeb receives cert+key over SSH (the only transport the appliance supports for key material); FortiADC over REST. The Admin GUI certificate can be swapped with a dry-run preview.
  • Lifecycle policy: the default rotation windows above, plus clean-up of expired and revoked material from devices, auto-apply or report-only. A Run sweep now button and a nightly scheduled action keep it moving; the page lists everything currently due, and each row shows its next step and when.

The ACME DNS-provider registry lives on the same settings tab (Settings → Certificate Manager), and it is a registry, not a fixed list. Each entry is a provider: a slug, a label, the flag the ACME client needs, a documentation link, an enable switch, a sort order, and its own list of credential fields. Because the field list is data, adding a DNS provider that was never shipped is a catalog entry, not a code change.

  • Credentials are saved per provider, into that provider's own named fields, and are never returned to the browser — the audit record names which variables were touched, never their values. Each field has an explicit clear tick, so emptying a credential is a decision rather than a side effect of leaving a box blank.
  • Built-in providers cannot be deleted — disable them instead; only entries you added are deletable.
  • The shipped catalog and any local additions are layered: the base file plus an overlay, so an update to the shipped list never discards your entries.

The node's own certificate is a different concern. This section is about certificates on the appliances. The certificate SATOM itself presents to your browser and to its peer is Settings → Node TLS (§26.8), and the CAs SATOM trusts when it dials an appliance are the trust store (§10.1). Three different questions, three different pages.

10.1 The trust store — the CAs SATOM itself trusts

Global → Settings → Trust store (admin).

Every appliance row carries a verify_ssl switch, and until this page existed it had only two positions: validate against the public roots — which an appliance signed by your own CA can never satisfy — or validate nothing. That is why the answer to "the new device never syncs" was always the same verify_ssl=false, including on devices where verification would have worked. This page is the missing third position: name the CA and keep the check on.

  • Import accepts a pasted PEM or an uploaded file, in two labelled boxes — Root CA and Intermediate CA. A whole chain in one blob is the normal case and is handled. Both boxes are submitted as a single transaction, so a root cannot land while its intermediate fails and leave behind a chain gap you never asked for.
  • The label is a hint, not the verdict. The role is derived from the certificate itself (self-issued ⇒ root), so a root pasted into the intermediate box is still recorded as a root. A form field must not be able to relabel a trust anchor.
  • Only CA certificates are accepted. A device's own self-signed leaf is refused, with the reason: nothing can anchor a chain on it, so importing it would appear to work and then fail every handshake.
  • The bundle adds to the public roots; it never replaces them. A mixed fleet — some devices behind your CA, others behind a publicly-signed wildcard — keeps working. If the bundle cannot be built at all, verification falls back to the public roots, never to off.
  • The page lists incomplete chains: an enabled intermediate whose issuer is in neither the store nor the public roots.
  • It is not only for appliances. Every connection SATOM opens to an address you configure verifies against the same bundle (public roots plus this store): the update feed and package index in Settings → General → Update sources (and the pip the updater runs), the git remote, SMTP, alert webhooks, LDAP / Active Directory, the secret vault (unless it names its own CA), NetBox, ticket trackers, DNS / IPAM providers, the AI and Sentinel endpoints, App-ID sources and integrations. An internal service signed by your CA needs nothing but its CA here. A connection whose verify TLS switch you turned off stays unverified.
  • Probe aims a real TLS handshake at any device visible in this ADOM and separates the three causes, because each needs a different fix: untrusted issuer (import a CA), hostname mismatch (correct the appliance's host, or reissue with that name in the SAN), and an expired leaf (reissue — no CA rescues it). "Verification failed" on its own is not an answer.

11. Backups & restore

  • Device Backups (FortiWeb ADOM → Operations) is the config-backup vault: every backup row shows filename, date, size, source (device/upload), firmware and author.
  • Create Backup offers a transport selector: Auto (REST first, SSH fallback), REST only, or SSH only (show full-configuration). Unlicensed/locked devices are still backed up via SSH.
  • Upload .conf files by hand, download or delete rows at will.
  • Permissions: View backups (backups.view, held by read-only too) lists the vault — metadata only; creating, uploading and deleting need Create or Restore backups (backups.create / backups.restore); a download needs backups.create, because it is the full device configuration. Buttons you cannot use are not shown.
  • Restore (appliance detail): pick a vault row and apply (FortiWeb). It needs Manage users and Restore backups (users.manage + backups.restore). Before a live restore a pre-restore safety backup is pulled over the device REST API; if it cannot be taken the restore is aborted, unless you tick Restore without a pre-restore backup (for a device whose REST backup cannot work, e.g. a backup password is set) — that choice is written to the audit log. For FortiADC the vault works (pull/upload/download) but config apply has no REST transport — the page says so honestly.
  • System Backup & Restore (Settings → Source of Truth & Backup) backs up the manager itself: a pg_dump of the database plus the reports tree in one bundle, with a verified restore path. Create backup now also pushes the bundle to the backup server when one is configured (the box is ticked by default). Code rollback on the same page is an update to an older commit and obeys the same staged-rollout safeguard as Software Update → Apply: on a primary with a standby, roll the standby back first. On a container install both code rollback and offline update packages are refused with the reason (deploy a new image tag instead).
  • Pre-upgrade/downgrade backups land in the same vault automatically.

Off-box copies — the source of truth and the external server. The vault above lives on this node. Two settings decide what leaves it:

  • Settings → Software Update Repository (§26.4) is the repository this node downloads its own code from. It is also the transport the shared release-notes corpus (§31.1) rides on. What still works when that remote is down, and how to recover afterwards, is git-backup-and-outage.md. It holds no device configuration and no firmware.
  • Settings → Backup Server (§26.5b) configures the external SFTP destination. That server is where the appliances push their own scheduled config backups, where retired firmware is archived, and it is the target of the push_server option on the system-backup action and the monitoring reports (§15, §14.9). The scheduled action device_inspect is the one that uploads the versioned source-of-truth blobs off-box.
  • Settings → Configuration SoT (§26.5) is where the retention of those blobs is set — and it is the only one of the three the word source of truth applies to.

How the local source of truth is versioned and what it does and does not hold: source-of-truth-spec.md.

Recovery custody — the sealed envelope. A bundle holds a pg_dump in which every appliance credential, the node identity key and the backup-server password are Fernet ciphertext. The key that opens them is FERNET_KEY in .env, and the internal CA key lives in pki/ — neither is in git, in the HA datasync or in any bundle, on purpose. The consequence is the part worth remembering: a bundle restored onto a rebuilt node is a database of unreadable secrets.

SATOM closes that without putting the key in the backup. Both secrets are wrapped in a scrypt+AES-GCM envelope at data/recovery/seal.json, which the datasync replicates to the peer within five minutes and every bundle carries off-box from then on. Whoever steals a bundle holds ciphertext; you, holding a passphrase and nothing else, can rebuild the installation from any copy.

  • The passphrase is minted at install, shown once, and never stored by the product. A secondary node inherits it through the join key, so both nodes open the same envelope. Write it down somewhere that is not the cluster — if it lives on the same disk as the node, you have three copies of a box you cannot open.
  • Seal on the primary, not the standby. Only the primary holds the internal CA key, so a standby seal would produce an envelope that cannot re-issue the replication mTLS; and the standby's data/ is overwritten from the primary every five minutes, so the file would not survive anyway.
  • Verbs: satom execute seal recovery (re-run at any time; it replaces rather than accumulates), satom execute unseal recovery, and satom diagnose recovery, which reports an absent, stale, unreadable or unreachable envelope. A node with no envelope is noisy on purpose.

11.1 Cloning one deploy into another

A bundle puts this deploy back the way it was. To copy a deploy's configuration into a different installation (lab → production, an old pair → a new one) use a clone: the two installations keep their own FERNET_KEY, their own identity and their own HA pair, and no key ever leaves either node.

  1. On the source primary: sudo satom execute clone export --yes. The bundle lands in data/clone-exports/ and the command prints a passphrase once — it is stored nowhere.
  2. Copy the file to the target primary. Both deploys must run the same SATOM version: the import compares the schema revision and every table's columns and refuses on any difference.
  3. On the target primary: sudo satom execute clone import <file> shows the plan; add --yes to run it (the passphrase is asked on the terminal, or read from $SATOM_CLONE_PASSPHRASE, never from argv).
  4. Check the appliances and schedules, make sure the source no longer acts on the same appliances, then sudo satom execute clone release --yes. satom get clone status says whether the node is still holding a clone.

What travels is configuration only: appliances and their credentials, users, profiles and settings, scheduled action definitions, templates, baselines, exceptions, probes and scrape targets, dashboards, the wiki, the API library; Script Library scripts and schedules; integration hooks; WAF artifacts; branding.

What stays behind:

Left behind Why
Backups: the device vault (data/backups/) and the system bundles backups, not configuration
Config history: the SoT store and the live config tree (data/reports/) history of the source's appliances
Device cache (objects, snapshots, certificates, hardware, NICs) the first sync after clone release reads it again from the appliances
Runs, logs, samples, incidents, notifications, change requests the target produces its own
Firmware images the target keeps its own
Queued script and hook requests the target would run them a second time

The list of left-behind tables is the target's, not the bundle's: a bundle that carries one of them is refused.

How the secrets travel: the export re-encrypts every Fernet token it finds — columns, settings and tokens inside JSON settings — under a one-time transfer key, and seals that key with the passphrase (scrypt + AES-GCM). The import opens it and re-encrypts every token under the target's own key, then checks that the target can open every token in the database and lists any it cannot. A secret kept in the external vault travels as its vault marker; the target reaches it through the same vault configuration, which travels with the bundle, and the export says how many there are.

What the target keeps: its HA role and peer, node certificate and identity key, backup server, signature store, recovery escrow and alert state. Accounts do not stay: after the import you log in with the source's users and passwords, and every browser session opened before the import is logged out — a session names a user by number, and the numbers now belong to the source's accounts.

The import replaces the target's configuration:

  • Before anything changes it checks every checksum, the passphrase and the schema, and refuses a bundle exported from this same deploy (use satom execute restore db for that). It refuses on a standby.
  • It takes a safety bundle of the current database, stops the web, scheduler and reconciler, and replaces the rows in one transaction. In the same transaction it empties the target's own history, device cache and backup index: those rows name appliances by number, and after the import the numbers belong to the source's appliances. The target's system bundles, firmware and signature store are kept.
  • It moves the replaced file sets, the target's device vault, live config tree and SoT store to data/clone-prev-<time>/ instead of deleting them; the directories themselves stay, empty, for the next sync and backup.
  • Until the first device sync after the release, the target shows the appliances without their objects.
  • The imported deploy starts held: every scheduled action, Script Library schedule and hook that was enabled is switched off, and so are alert e-mail and the NetBox push. Two installations polling and writing the same appliances is what a clone otherwise produces without anyone noticing. clone release switches back on exactly what was held — what was already off on the source stays off — and computes each schedule's next run from now, so the held period is not replayed.
  • Rollback: satom execute restore db <safety bundle> --yes, and the previous file sets from data/clone-prev-<time>/.

From the console: Settings → Source of Truth & Backup → Deploy Clone (admins, user_manage) does the same four steps without a shell. It is not Clone / Migrate under Fleet & Devices, which copies configuration between appliances.

  • Export queues the export and shows the passphrase once, in the page, at the moment you click. The finished bundle is listed with a download button.
  • Upload puts a bundle into the target's import inbox (data/clone-imports/) and shows what it would bring: source node and version, tables, rows, file sets, and every reason it cannot be imported here (a different schema, a bundle from this same deploy). Uploads through the page stop at the front end's limit (400 MB on a standard install); copy larger bundles to the node and use the CLI.
  • Import asks for the passphrase and for IMPORT typed out, checks the passphrase before it queues anything, then runs. Your session ends with everyone else's: log in again with the source's account, and Recent clone jobs shows each step of the import.
  • Release (shown while the deploy is held) needs RELEASE typed out.

Export and import do not run in the web process. They are queued for the privileged runner (satom-updater), which runs the installed CLI — the same code as the commands above — because an import has to stop the web service that is serving the page. The passphrase reaches the runner in the request file only. The runner deletes that file before it does anything else, the HA datasync does not copy that directory, and the passphrase is never written to a job's status. On a standby the pane is read-only. In the container runtime the pane is read-only too, because there is no privileged runner there. A job the runner cannot finish within 25 minutes is stopped, and the web, scheduler and reconciler are started again; run imports that big from a shell.

A clone copies a deploy's whole configuration; copying only some of it (by category or by appliance) into a deploy that keeps its own data is not available yet.

Diagnose Log Collection (under Operations › Troubleshooting) and Import Backup (next to Device Backups under Operations) are covered in §27. Neither is a backup: one collects read-only diagnostics over SSH, the other parses a config file entirely offline.

12. Firmware upgrades

Appliance detail → Upgrade (FortiWeb and FortiADC):

  1. Upload the .out image (or pick a previously uploaded one).
  2. The runbook takes a mandatory config backup, probes every published service before, pushes the image, monitors the reboot/recovery, probes after, and produces a before/after diff plus a status page.
  3. Release-notes advisory: the app maintains a harvested corpus of vendor known/resolved issues; the advisor diffs current → target so you see what the upgrade fixes and what it inherits.
  4. Unattended (scheduled) upgrades only ever run inside an approved Change Request window (§15) — there is no way to schedule a flash without an approval. The scheduled path is Upgrade Flow; the Upgrade page itself flashes now and has no "Schedule for later" card any more.
  5. Boot partition (flash the alternate partition / roll back) is the emergency path: it does not need a change request, so it can roll back a change that went wrong outside any window. A live flash requires ticking "I understand this live flash bypasses change control" and typing the appliance name; the attempt (refused or started) and its outcome are written to the audit log.

FortiADC takes the same steps with its own transport, the one its GUI uses: the image goes to the box's inactive partition and the box reboots into it, so there is no maturity question and no partition to choose. The Boot Partition page of a FortiADC also shows both partitions and, when the inactive one holds a build, offers Boot alternate partition: a reboot into that build with no image sent — the quick rollback. Same gates as the emergency flash (acknowledgement + typed name, audited), and it is refused before anything is sent when the inactive partition is empty. The FortiADC API console and scheduled custom REST calls refuse the paths that change the box even on a GET (reboot, shutdown, factory reset, partition swap, restore, image upload): use these pages instead.

The Firmware library (Administrator → Firmware, admin) is the store the upgrade step 1 picks from, and it is worth using rather than re-uploading an image per device.

  • Each row is an image with its version, build, product, platform (hardware / VM / any), size, uploader, notes and a sha256 recorded at upload. The binary lives on disk; the database row keeps the metadata and the hash, so integrity is checkable later.
  • Platform is detected from the file name. Fortinet's naming carries it: FWB_KVM-…, FGT_VM64_KVM-… or FAD_VM-… is a VM image, FWB_1000E-… or FGT_60F-… a hardware one. Choosing the file fills Platform (and the hypervisor of an install image) and marks it "detected from the file name"; uploads and backup-server pulls apply the same rule on the server. A platform you pick yourself is kept, and a name that does not say stays Any. When an image is offered to an appliance, the appliance's probed hardware type decides the match (its model string only when it was never probed).
  • Uploads keep running while you navigate. A firmware image is hundreds of megabytes; it goes up as one request that the Jobs dock tracks across page changes, and the sha256 is computed by a background job once the file has landed.
  • The page is ADOM-scoped at the query, not in the template — a FortiWeb workspace sees FortiWeb images and Global sees everything, and a hidden row was never fetched in the first place. Inside a concrete ADOM the product is not offered as a choice, because the upload handler would overrule it anyway.
  • Two artefact families, kept apart: kind Upgrade (.out, applies to a running appliance) and kind Install (a hypervisor image, builds a new machine — see 21.5). Choosing the wrong one is the mistake this field exists to prevent.
  • Images are downloadable and deletable, and a JSON manifest of the library is published for the console and the provisioning runs to read.
  • Which ADOMs offer a Firmware page at all is the firmware capability on the ADOM registry (§26.11), so a newly firmware-capable workspace appears without a code change.

13. Fleet tools

All in the Global ADOM (also linked from the product Operations groups):

13.0 Architecture: drawing the path, reading the devices

Operations → Architecture (/net-architecture/) is the drawn counterpart of the Service Diagram. The Service Diagram is derived from the FortiWeb cache; an Architecture drawing is what you say the network is, and SATOM checks it against what the devices say.

  • Drawing. Take an element from the Elements palette, drag it into place, Link two elements and fill the inspector on the right (label, IP or CIDR, VLAN tag, the SATOM appliance it is, a probe URL). There is no Save button: every change saves itself (see Autosave below). Saving needs config_write; viewing does not. A drawing holds at most 300 elements and 600 links. A drawing with any error — a link to an element that is not there, two elements with one id, a CIDR that is not a network, a binding to a device of the wrong kind — is refused whole and nothing is stored.
  • Networks behind a firewall. A LAN or segment element names the FortiGate element it sits behind and, optionally, the interface (port2). Without an interface name, the segment is matched to the FortiGate port whose address its CIDR contains. That binding is what puts firewall policies on the drawing.
  • Read devices reads, now and read-only, every bound FortiGate the current ADOM can see (tick every 30 s to repeat it while the page is open): its interfaces (address, link, RX/TX) and its policies (interfaces, addresses, services, action, NAT, hit count, bytes, last use), plus the implicit-deny counter. Each policy is drawn as an arrow from its source segment to its destination segment (green accept, red deny); click a policy in the inspector to light up its path. A policy whose interface has nothing drawn behind it says not drawn: portN instead of disappearing. A bound FortiWeb shows its server policies from SATOM's device cache (no live read); FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator and FortiAnalyzer elements get their links, nothing is read from them. Any element with a probe URL — a back-end, a management host, any other host — gets one HTTP GET from SATOM (status, latency, one response header of your choice); the probe does not verify TLS and does not follow redirects. Nothing read is stored or cached.
  • Scope. An element bound to a device of another ADOM is drawn but not read or linked; each product ADOM sees only its own appliances, so a drawing that mixes products is fully readable only from the Global ADOM. Binding an element to a device you cannot see is refused on save.
  • Path Diagnostics and Sentinel. A bound device element links to its Device page, to Path Diagnostics with that appliance already selected, and to Sentinel.
  • Layers. L2 draws ports, MAC, speed, link state (green up, red down) and VLAN on the firewall links, and on each host the MAC the FortiGate learned for its address. L3 shows addresses, routes and the policy flows. L4 labels each policy with its services, active sessions and hits. L7 draws FortiWeb server policies (from the device cache) to the drawn back-ends they publish and shows the HTTP probe answers.
  • Trace a flow. Enter source, destination, protocol and port (or use Trace from here / to here on a host). Each FortiGate on the way is asked for its route to both ends and for its own policy lookup; the path is drawn in colour (cyan allowed, red denied, amber unknown) and the inspector lists each firewall with ingress → egress interface, matched policy and action. A firewall that cannot be read is listed with its error, never skipped. A public address with no network drawn for it lands on the Internet element. TCP traces through a FortiWeb or FortiADC offer Validate with Path Diagnostics. A trace stops after six firewalls ("more than 6 firewalls: stopped"), and every trace is written to the audit log as netarch.trace.
  • Adding elements. Elements opens a palette with every appliance of the fleet the ADOM can see (one click adds it, bound and addressed) and the generic types.
  • Autosave, undo, team work. Changes save themselves; Undo/Redo (and Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z) step through them. Every save carries the version it was based on: if a colleague saved in between, their drawing is shown and yours stays one Undo away. Open pages refresh to a colleague's save within 15 seconds.

  • What it cannot see. Switches: draw the segments they carry. A FortiGate is read over REST with the token SATOM already holds.

  • Architecture — network diagrams you draw yourself (§13.0). Place the elements of a service path (Internet, LAN, segments/VLANs, FortiGate, FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer, back-end servers, management hosts), link them, and SATOM lays the devices' own data on top: FortiGate interfaces and policies with hit counters, each policy drawn from its source segment to its destination segment, and an HTTP probe of every back-end with a URL. Device elements link to Path Diagnostics and Sentinel.

  • Service Diagram — an SVG network-design diagram of the whole fleet: Internet → published services (VIP:port, TLS lock) → appliance chassis → pools → backend stacks, grouped in zones. Hover lights up a service's full path; search (IP/device/policy/profile/pool) focuses the view; click any node for the full cached detail with deep links into configuration. Filters: zone / line / department / kind / firmware / protocol / WAF / policy state — saved per user.
  • Search — fleet-wide full-text search over the cached configs and policy reports (names, VIPs, backend IPs, certificates, comments…).
  • Fleet Objects — typed, cross-device object listings (server policies, WAF profiles, pools…) with filters and CSV export, plus a generic any-field search over the entire cache.
  • WAF: the fleet-wide FortiWeb picture, in six read-only pages (Overview, Inventory, Profiles, Coverage, Artifacts, Exceptions; §13.1). It is a submenu of the Global menu and of the FortiWeb ADOM's Operations group. In the FortiWeb ADOM it also holds the device-scoped WAF tools (§13.2). The other ADOMs have no WAF submenu, because they have no FortiWeb objects to count.
  • Analysis — product-specific by design. A load balancer, a WAF and an identity server do not have the same failure modes, so each ADOM gets a page written against the objects that product actually has. There is no shared fallback: a workspace whose analyser is not written yet says so instead of showing another product's empty panels.
ADOM What Analysis shows
FortiWeb FortiView traffic/sources per device with filtering, plus an assisted packet capture builder that runs the appliance sniffer over SSH and hands you a Wireshark bundle (.pcap + TLS key log for decryption)
FortiADC Delivery posture from the cached config: virtual servers and their published services, pools with member counts and health-check coverage, real servers, the security profiles each virtual server references (WAF / IPS / AV / DoS), client-SSL profiles and local certificate expiry
FortiAuthenticator Entitlement first — licensed users, groups, FSSO and SSO-mobility seats used against their ceiling, FortiToken stock, then identity inventory (local/remote users, groups, RADIUS and TACACS+ clients, issued certificates) and unit posture
FortiAnalyzer Its own FortiView group inside the workspace menu (§17.3)

Every finding names the object it came from, and the page reads the local cache only — it opens with the appliance switched off, and it keeps working when the device's configuration API is refusing calls. - DNS & LB Lookup — resolve any name against your configured DNS servers (AdGuard/OPNsense/etc., admin-configurable list) and simultaneously match it against the fleet's load-balancing config: which policy/virtual server publishes it, with a mini policy→pool→backend graph and config deep links. - Where these live: Backend Reachability, Config Compare, Path Diagnostics, the Transaction Tracer (§37.3) and Scout sit together under Operations › Troubleshooting in every ADOM (since 2026-10-14; the tracer since 2026-10-16 — before that it was a window in the header Tools menu). The FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator ADOMs list only the Transaction Tracer and Scout from this set, because the other three work on FortiWeb and FortiADC objects. Diagnose Log Collection is also in Troubleshooting, in all five device ADOMs (§27.1). - Backend Reachability — paste or upload a list of source;policy;destination lines and ask one question per line: do the real servers behind this policy answer, on the source box and then on the destination box? It needs no workspace tab open and no appliance selected, and it writes nothing — the pool members are read back from each device and probed, never planned or copied.

Two vantages, never merged into one word: this node over TCP to the member's real port (always available; a refused port proves the host is up), and optionally each appliance over execute ping (needs SSH, off by default, and it is the only vantage that says whether that box has a route). Three answers, never two — a backend nobody could probe is reported unknown, never as an outage and never as health.

Per line you get a verdict — ok · down · mismatch · unknown · error — plus every finding that earned it: unreachable members, a pool the destination is missing a member from, a policy that is not on one of the boxes. A destination that cannot be resolved or read does not void the source half. When the destination does not have the policy at all and SSH is on, the source's backends are pinged from the destination instead — the pre-migration question — and that side is labelled as the different measurement it is.

Lines starting with # are ignored; a third field left empty checks the source only; up to 200 lines per run. Anything the run could not cover (an expired time budget, the target cap, an over-limit line) is named in the report rather than quietly omitted. The result copies out as TSV. - Config Compare — paste or upload the same source;policy;destination list and ask the next question about those services: is this configured the same on both boxes, and if not, what exactly differs? Every object behind the policy is read on both appliances and subtracted — virtual server, pool and its members, certificates, content routing, allow-lists, the web protection profile. It needs no workspace tab open and no appliance selected, and it writes nothing.

Objects are matched by the field that references them, not by their name. A profile or pool that landed on the destination under a derived name still lines up with its counterpart and is reported renamed — one finding, rather than one object missing plus another appearing. A rename is never repeated as configuration drift on the parent that points at it.

A web protection profile is compared as one package. You get its fingerprint on each side, how many objects it holds, and which sub-profiles differ (−removed ~changed +added) — never a row per signature or entry. The package's own name is outside the fingerprint, so a renamed profile whose contents match reads as renamed, not as a wall of differences.

The comparison is symmetric: a setting only the destination carries is reported exactly like one only the source carries. Per-box bookkeeping is not — a sub-table row's appliance-assigned id never decides whether two rows are the same row, and enable/True, 80/"80", absent/empty are each one value.

Per line you get a verdict — identical · differs · missing · error — and, for missing, which box does not have the policy at all. Lines starting with # are ignored; both sides are required (a comparison needs two); up to 100 lines per run, because one line is two full dependency-tree reads. Any line the time budget did not reach is named in the report, never dropped. Export is tab-separated, one line per difference. - Monitoring / Metrics — see §14.

13.1 Operations → WAF: the fleet-wide pages

Operations → WAF shows every FortiWeb this console can see on one set of pages. In the Global console that is every FortiWeb; in the FortiWeb ADOM, that ADOM's own boxes. Every page needs protection.view and writes nothing. The pages read the source-of-truth snapshots the hourly harvest already took, so opening them contacts no appliance. The figures are therefore only as recent as the last harvest, and freshness is shown on every page:

  • A snapshot older than 26 hours is still shown but marked stale.
  • A device that was never harvested is listed as missing. It is not counted as zero policies and is left out of the denominators.
  • The page says how many devices actually reported.
Page What it answers
Overview (/waf/) KPI tiles and What this fleet would want fixed: policies in monitor mode, with no web protection profile, administratively disabled, or naming a profile missing from the snapshot; TLS policies with no certificate or still accepting TLS 1.0/1.1; custom profiles no policy uses. Six charts (enforcement posture, transport security, protection coverage, signature policy in use, policies per device/ADOM, configuration changes over the last 30 days) and a snapshot-freshness table.
Inventory Every server policy in the fleet, with its enforcement (Blocking, Detection only, No profile, Disabled), TLS, certificate, virtual server, pool, profile and signature policy. Filters: device/ADOM, enforcement, TLS (plain / weak / TLS), free text. CSV export.
Profiles Every web protection profile: custom or predefined, how many policies use it, protections on against slots available. Filter to orphan (custom, used by no policy) or used. CSV export.
Coverage A protection × device/ADOM matrix of on / applicable. A profile that has no slot for a protection is left out of that protection's denominator, not counted as "off". CSV export.
Artifacts File-backed objects (schemas, WSDL, OpenAPI files…) across the fleet, read from the artifact index. For each one: what the estate needs, what SATOM holds, and so what could not be migrated today. States: Held, Blocked, At risk, Borrowed, Orphan copy, Library copy. CSV export.
Exceptions Every carve-out authored in SATOM on every visible device, and which devices hold it. Carve-outs are grouped by their declared library link, or else by identical content. Also listed: stale carve-outs, carve-outs that predate versioning (they cannot be rolled back), and orphans whose appliance is gone. These are authored carve-outs, not device state: a carve-out is live only on a box where someone pushed it. CSV export.

On Artifacts and Exceptions, the filters narrow the table only. The tiles and charts above it always describe the whole visible fleet.

Operations → WAF → Overview: KPIs and "What this fleet would want fixed"; the sidebar shows the WAF submenu of the FortiWeb ADOM

Export. Every WAF page has an export panel. Tick the datasets you want (overview figures and charts, server policies, web protection profiles, protection coverage, artifacts, exceptions with their profiles) and the formats (CSV with one file per dataset, an Excel workbook, a PDF report with charts). You get one ZIP.

  • The selection is in the URL, so you can bookmark a bundle.
  • If nothing is ticked, the page warns you and produces no file.
  • Each export is recorded in the audit log as waf.export.

13.2 Operations → WAF in the FortiWeb ADOM: the device tools

In the FortiWeb ADOM, the WAF submenu also holds the three device-scoped WAF tools. They used to sit in the ADOM's own WAF group, which no longer exists. Their URLs and permissions did not change. The Global console's WAF submenu does not list them, because they are FortiWeb-ADOM pages and a link from Global would switch the tab's ADOM.

Entry URL Device
Search Attack ID (§9.1) /waf/attack-search/ Not needed: the block-page reference names the appliance, or you pick it on the page
Exceptions & Signature (§9) /web/exceptions/<device id> Needed. With none selected, /web/exceptions/ sends you to the Service Diagram
WAF Artifacts: Object types · Inventory · Device audit /artifacts/, /artifacts/inventory, /artifacts/audit Needed. With none selected, each page sends you to the Service Diagram with "Pick a device first"

WAF Artifacts is a collapsible entry with three pages. Each page shows one device and ADOM: the device selected in the sidebar (§3.1). No control widens it to the fleet; for the fleet-wide view, use Operations → WAF → Artifacts (§13.1).

  • Object types: statistics for the selected device and ADOM, per object type, with the reference for each type.
  • Inventory: every file-backed object the device and ADOM holds, the policies and profiles that use it, and what would block a move. The Upload a file, Author content and Capture from device buttons add a version to SATOM's artifact store and need config_write.
  • Device audit: what SATOM knows about the device's artifacts, on screen, as JSON or as CSV. The CSV has one row per device, policy, profile and artifact. It reads only SATOM's index and contacts no appliance. The report itself warns that a policy created since the last sweep is missing from it.

XML Schema, WSDL and gRPC IDL can't be read back off a FortiWeb one object at a time. The device's Entire configuration backup does carry their content, but inside a block the firmware encrypts even without a backup password, and restoring that backup does not put them back: measured on 7.6.8 and 8.0.6, in both directions, the restore brings the configuration back and drops every XML Schema and WSDL object, name included. To move one of these objects, upload the original file (from the team that owns the API), or fetch it from the service.

Fetch from the application (Inventory) is the way in for a FortiWeb already in production. Give the URL where the SOAP service publishes its WSDL or XML Schema (often the service address followed by ?wsdl) and the object name the policy already references. SATOM downloads it, follows the schemas it imports or includes from the same host, and stores each one as a version with the origin fetched. It never writes to the appliance. It refuses non-http(s) URLs, credentials in the URL, documents with a DTD, loopback, link-local and SATOM's own addresses; it reports redirects and references to other hosts instead of following them, and stops at 25 documents, 5 levels or 60 seconds. Imported schemas are named after their file; check the names against what the policy needs (Needed by a policy and NOT held).

FortiWeb checks a schema's references when the file is uploaded, and looks a relative schemaLocation up as an XML Schema object on the device, by name. So SATOM rewrites every reference it followed to the name it stored that document under, and says so in the version note. A reference it did not follow is kept as written and listed in the result: the appliance resolves it itself at upload, and refuses the file if it can't. On the device, a schema has to exist before the schema or WSDL that imports it.

A clone or migration takes care of that order. Before the first write it reads the WSDL and XML Schema content it is about to upload and, for every schema that content imports: moves it ahead if the plan already creates it, leaves it alone if the destination already holds it, and otherwise adds it to the plan right before the importing file, with the copy SATOM holds. The pre-flight lists those schemas and which file imports each one; one SATOM can't supply is a missing file like any other, and the files that import it are skipped.

On FortiWeb 8.0.6 build0116 every gRPC IDL upload fails with errcode -3000: Internal error processing requested file, whatever the file; 7.6.8 accepts the same file. SATOM adds that note to the error.

Operations → WAF → WAF Artifacts → Inventory for the selected device

13.3 Naming: Scheme and Discovery

Administrator → Naming is in every device ADOM (FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiGate, FortiAuthenticator, FortiAnalyzer). Its two tabs work on one list of object types: every table the product's configuration sync reads, including the ones no device holds an object of yet. Settings blocks are not object types and are left out: rows without a name, and an empty endpoint the API library measured as one settings object on the devices' builds, or that the FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator sync saw answer as one object (those syncs record whether each table answered a list, even an empty one, or one object). An empty type nothing has measured yet stays listed and is marked list or settings block not measured. A table whose objects are keyed by number is listed and marked so.

Scheme holds the pattern of each object type. Entries marked builds names (the FortiWeb catalog: server policy, pool, WPP, certificate…) are the ones SATOM fills in when it creates objects from a web address, so they take the site tokens and the product's variables only (Managed Certificate: {class} {cn} {date} {serial}; Exception WPP: {name}, the policy's name). Every other entry documents your convention and may use any Discovery token.

The site tokens:

Token Value for https://Blabla.Example.com:8443/x
{name} blabla-example-com — the slug, as before
{host} blabla.example.com — the host as typed, dots kept
{port} the port the creating flow gives (the wizard's Port), else 8443 from the address

Variables (the table above the patterns, one list per product) rewrite a token with a regular expression so the name is one the devices accept. Each row has a name, the token it reads (a site token or a variable above it, never one below), a regular expression (Python syntax, every match replaced, \1 for a group) and what to replace with. Use it in a pattern as {its_name}. Example: host_u reads host, replaces \. with _; the pattern {host_u}-{port} gives blabla_example_com-443. The Sample web address and Port fields preview every pattern live; the token values come from the server, so the preview is what the wizard will build. A variable list that cannot be computed (a reserved name such as num, an unknown source, a regex that does not compile, a \2 with one group) saves nothing, and removing a variable a pattern still uses is refused with the pattern named. Restore defaults resets the patterns and keeps the variables. FortiADC works the same way with its own list; no SATOM flow builds FortiADC names yet, so there they are a reference a future flow uses as is. Existing names are checked against a catalog pattern with {host} and every variable read as free text. Next to each input: what Discovery found on the devices (all devices agree / devices differ), use it to copy it in, and a live count of the existing names that follow the pattern you type. Use the filter box or Only types with objects on a device to narrow the list.

Discovery reads the names already on a device — from the configuration tree SATOM keeps for it, no device call — and shows, per object type:

  • Convention found — the dominant pattern, e.g. pol-{adom}-{name} or vs-{name}-{proto}, with any variant prefix, the separator and the case.
  • Follow it — how many of the team's objects match it.
  • Naming scheme — the scheme's pattern for that type and how many objects follow it ((default) when it is the catalog default).
  • Exceptions, each with its reason. A stale name is the one to read first: name says 'https' but the object's port is '8080'.
  • Shares {name} with — object types that carry the same identifier through a real reference (policy → pool → virtual server).
  • Vendor — factory objects, counted apart and never used to infer anything (device flag first, then a factory-name list measured per product, then physical ports).

A part of a name becomes {port}, {proto}, {adom}, {host}… only when it equals a field of the same object on at least 80 % of the objects; digits that match nothing are {num}; the free part is {name}. One object is "too few".

Adopt writes the discovered pattern into the scheme entry of that object type. Adopt & adapt opens it in an editor under the row: change a part (lab-spo-{num} → spo-{name}), watch how many names follow, then Save to scheme. For a builds names entry, Adopt is greyed out when the found pattern carries a token SATOM cannot fill in (hover for the reason) — adapt it instead. The ✕ clears the entry. All devices (fleet view) shows whether the devices agree and your scheme pattern; Export CSV lists every exception. A device without a configuration tree offers Sync device (read-only).

14. Monitoring: fleet health, metrics & probes

Monitoring lives in every workspace, not only Global. It is scoped by device kind, so the FortiWeb workspace shows FortiWeb appliances and nothing about the manager itself. Three submenus, and they answer three different questions.

14.1 Fleet health — is the box alive?

One card per appliance. The badge is the worst of four independent signals, and every signal that is not healthy is printed underneath, so a state is never unexplained:

Signal Warns Critical
Harvest — the last scheduled config syncs one failed run three failed runs in a row
Cache — the newest stored snapshot nothing cached, or older than monitoring.stale_hours (6 h) older than 4× that
Probes — the enabled monitors for that device a probe alerting, or all probes disabled a probe critical
Capacity — object-count headroom against the admin cap over capacity.warn_pct over capacity.crit_pct

Two rules matter when reading it:

  • unknown is not ok. A device nothing has been measured about renders unknown, never healthy.
  • A disabled probe is not a passing probe. Switching off a monitor that always fails removes coverage, and the card says so rather than turning green.

When a deep monitor is what makes a device degraded or critical, the alert says what was measured and against which line. The title carries the reading and the limit crossed (Device {device} is critical — CPU 97.0% (critical 95%)), and the body lists each alerting probe: what it measures (for CPU and memory, the whole appliance), the last reading, every limit it is graded against with where that limit is set (set on this probe, inherited from fortiweb, factory default) and when it was read. Six probes are spelled out; the rest are counted. The in-app notification keeps the line breaks.

Appliances in maintenance are marked as such and are skipped by automatic runs and by their alerts. That is the correct way to silence a box you know is down — not lowering the alert floor.

Fleet health is two pages, each a direct entry of the Monitoring menu (there is no "Fleet health" sub-menu), because a number is read as a claim about the page it sits on:

  • Device health (/monitoring/) — the appliance cards above. Present in every workspace, scoped to that workspace's device kind. On a new node, never harvested / probes have never run usually means nothing is scheduled to do that work: the reason then ends with no 'device_sync' schedule on this node (or deep_monitor) and the command that creates the schedules, sudo satom execute seed actions --yes.
  • SATOM health (/monitoring/satom) — the installation itself: cluster peers, repository, external backup server, database, systemd units, redundancy, the host machine and Encryption in transit, where every badge is backed by a live probe rather than by configuration. Global only — a product workspace does not reach it, because those cards carry node hostnames and infrastructure addresses.

The host machine row grades disk, memory and CPU on both HA nodes, and it exists because nothing in the product used to measure its own box. Its limits live in Settings → Thresholds under the SATOM machine scope. CPU is the share of the node's own cores busy (0–100 %; warning 80, critical 95). Disk is the share of the space a non-root writer can use, the figure df prints: the ~5 % ext4 keeps for root is left out, because PostgreSQL is not root. The hypervisor's load average is shown next to it, labelled as the host's, and is not graded. Disk turns critical at 92 %, deliberately below 95: a full filesystem stops PostgreSQL writing WAL, so the alert has to arrive while there is still room to act on it.

Resource history, under the node tiles, keeps those same readings over time: one chart each for CPU, Memory and Disk, with every node on each chart, over 1 h, 6 h, 24 h, 7 days, 30 days or 90 days. The dashed lines are the warning and critical limits from Settings → Thresholds, so a chart shows the same line the alert fires on.

  • The readings are sampled by the metrics_scrape scheduled action (every 3 minutes) and stored in the local metrics store as the satom_node_* series, mirrored to the peer's store like every other series, so a promoted standby keeps the history. If metrics_scrape is paused, the charts stop growing; its run summary says N node sample(s), or node resources NOT recorded with the reason.
  • A node that did not answer leaves a gap, never a line carried forward, and writes satom_node_up 0. Each point looks back one interval plus six minutes, because the action fires every 3 to 6 minutes, so a gap means no reading for longer than that, not one late scrape.
  • Each point is the highest reading in its interval, so a short peak is not smoothed away on the long ranges. CPU is the share of the container's cores busy since the node's previous reading.
  • If the metrics store does not answer, the section says so in red instead of drawing empty charts.

The same data is available to an outside monitoring system through GET /api/v1/system/nodes (now) and GET /api/v1/system/nodes/history (over time), with a read token bound to the global ADOM — see the API v1 manual, §9.

14.2 Metrics — how much does it hold, and who changed it?

Monitoring → Metrics. Inventory counts and activity for the active workspace, over a date range. Nothing here touches an appliance — it reads the local cache, the audit log and the change history, so it opens with the whole fleet off.

Four inventory cards, labelled per ADOM rather than shared: FortiWeb counts Server Policies / Backends / WPPs / Certificates, FortiADC counts Virtual Servers / Real Servers / Server Pools / Certificates, FortiAuthenticator counts Users / Groups / RADIUS clients / Certificates, FortiAnalyzer counts Devices / Log sources / Reports / Certificates. The totals are rendered server-side, so the cards are still there if the charts fail to draw.

Where the totals come from differs by product, and the page will not fake it. FortiWeb and Global read the daily typed snapshots written by the inventory_snapshot scheduled action (§15) — which is why that action has to be scheduled daily for the trend to exist at all. New installations seed it daily at 23:50 (satom execute seed actions); on an older node the same command adds it. FortiADC has no snapshot pipeline, so its totals are counted live off the fleet and cached briefly. A product with neither reports no totals rather than borrowing another product's: an ADOM printing FortiWeb's object counts under its own labels is worse than printing nothing, because the numbers look like its own.

Activity over the range: total audited actions, real (non-dry-run) config changes, distinct active users, and how many appliances were actually touched — plus a breakdown of changes by object category (server policy, backend, WAF profile, certificate, other) derived from the endpoint each change hit.

Ranges and comparison: 7 / 30 / 90 days or a custom window, with a compare toggle that puts the immediately preceding window of the same length beside it — so "is this a busy week" has an answer rather than a number.

It is ADOM-scoped, precisely. Audit rows carry their own product stamp; change-history rows are scoped through the kind of the appliance they were made on, by inclusion rather than exclusion. Manager-level changes with no appliance count under FortiWeb, which is where they originate. Global sees everything.

14.3 Deep monitors — is the service still serving?

Monitoring → Deep monitors. These reach into the appliance (synthetic request or read-only CLI over SSH):

Kind What it records
Service policy (HTTPS) A synthetic request to a published front end: status, latency and days of certificate left. One 200 proves interface, policy, proxy daemon and backend at once. A sweep sends these requests concurrently (up to 16 at a time), and a front end that refuses or times out the connection is not contacted a second time for its certificate
Interface IP / link A name → address/state fingerprint per port. The drift against the previous sample is the event; an address change grades critical
Processor load / Memory usage Read from the appliance's own performance summary
proxyd process Worker count, memory used and free, and the set of process IDs — a different PID is a silent restart, which no ordinary health check shows

Not every kind fits every product, and the form says so rather than measuring zero. Service policy, processor load and memory usage are offered on FortiWeb, FortiADC and FortiAuthenticator; interface and proxyd are FortiWeb-only. On FortiAuthenticator, load and memory are read from the unit's REST status resource, not the CLI — the FAC shell answers No such command. to the performance summary, which is a successful round trip carrying no reading, exactly the kind of silence a monitor must never grade as healthy.

14.4 Service monitor — telemetry over the API

Monitoring → Service monitor. Same engine, no shell access — these read the appliance's monitoring API only, which means they keep working on a device whose configuration API is refusing calls (an expired licence, typically):

Kind Unit
Concurrent sessions (box) sessions, plus connections per second
Server-policy sessions & latency sessions, round-trip and application response time, per-member backend health
HTTP throughput Mbps, graded on the peak of the window, not the average
HTTP transactions transactions per bucket

On FortiAuthenticator the ceiling is not bandwidth, it is entitlement, so the kinds are different:

Kind Unit
Licence headroom % of the licensed user / group / FSSO / SSO-mobility seats consumed, with the free count spelled out
FortiToken pool % of the imported token stock already assigned

Both grade on percent consumed — same direction as every other probe in the product, so a threshold never has to be read backwards. A counter with no ceiling, or a pool with no tokens imported, reports unknown: neither is health.

The page also groups results per device: a traffic card per appliance and a per-policy detail view, both served from stored samples.

Reading sessions on short-lived HTTP. Connections per second is the number that moves; concurrent sessions can sit near zero under heavy load because each request lives microseconds. A threshold on policy_sessions grades sessions — for HTTP front ends, watch the throughput probe instead.

14.5 Creating probes

  • Discover from device offers the sets that apply to that product: published policies, a baseline, one probe per interface, or the API telemetry set on FortiWeb; a baseline plus the entitlement set on FortiAuthenticator. Ports and policy names are picked from the cached configuration, so the dialog opens with the appliance switched off.
  • Published policies are dialled once before their probe is created. A front end SATOM cannot connect to (a VIP that nothing routes from SATOM's network, such as a lab address or a front end only reachable from the client side) gets its probe disabled. The reason is shown in its Last result, and the discovery message counts these probes as "created disabled: VIP not reachable from SATOM". A disabled probe does not count in Device health. Enable it once SATOM can reach the VIP. A front end that connects but answers badly (timeout after connecting, HTTP 5xx) is created enabled, because that is a finding about the service. Policies that are disabled on the device are not dialled.
  • Every device gets the baseline (interfaces, CPU, memory, and proxyd on FortiWeb) without anyone pressing Discover. It is created when the device is added, whether from the form, the REST API (POST /api/appliances) or a provisioning run. The 3-minute Collection sweep also gives it to any device that still has no probe at all. Deleting one probe of a provisioned device is respected and the sweep does not put it back. To stop monitoring a device completely, disable its probes rather than deleting them all.
  • Interval must be a multiple of the sweep (3 minutes). A probe only fires when its own interval has elapsed and a sweep tick happens, so a 5-minute probe under a 3-minute sweep would really run every 6 minutes.
  • Probe now runs the current page's probes for the visible devices. It runs in the background and stays out of the progress dock — only a sweep that fails raises a notification.
  • Editing a probe is the pencil icon in the table.

14.6 History and charts

Click any sparkline for the drill-down: 1 h / 24 h / 7 d / 30 d or a custom range, with minimum / average / maximum, a healthy percentage, sample and transition counts, threshold lines and a per-bucket status strip.

Raw samples are capped per probe (retention, ~2 days at the default). Charts go further because every run also writes roll-ups: hourly kept 90 days, daily kept two years, storing min/avg/max rather than a mean — a four-minute spike is invisible in an average and is usually the reason the chart is open. The footer states which table was drawn, because an hourly mean and a three-minute reading are not the same claim about the appliance.

Changing a probe's unit resets its series. If a probe starts reporting a different quantity, its old samples are cleared rather than plotted on the same axis. That is a deliberate, manual operation — never a side effect of a restart.

14.7 Collection — the metrics store

Monitoring → Collection (needs config-write).

How many devices fits on this node, and how much disk will that take? Both questions have a formula, built from constants measured on a running node: Sizing a node. The short version is that the ceiling is device I/O, not storage — a node spends about 0.82 s per device in each 3-minute window, which puts ~110 devices on one installation — and that the intervals and top-N values on THIS page are the two dials that move it.

A probe asks one question. That is the right shape for "is this one thing still working" and the wrong shape for a fleet: at scale it becomes one API call per object per sweep. A collector asks once per device and keeps everything that came back — policies returns every policy on the box in a single call. So the unit here is (device, collector), never (device, object): the table stays roughly one row per device per collector no matter how many policies the fleet grows.

Collector Products Default interval
box — CPU, memory, sessions FortiWeb, FortiADC, FortiAuthenticator 3 min
capacity — licence headroom, FortiToken pools FortiAuthenticator 3 min
policies — sessions / conn rate / RTT, every policy FortiWeb 3 min
interfaces — link state and byte counters FortiWeb 3 min
traffic — device total plus top-N policies FortiWeb 15 min
transactions — HTTP transactions, top-N policies FortiWeb 60 min
vservers — virtual servers: sessions / RTT / pool health, every VS FortiADC 3 min
identity — accounts, groups, tokens, certificates, RADIUS/TACACS+ clients FortiAuthenticator 15 min
faz — log volume, storage, alerts, incidents, devices, task queue FortiAnalyzer 15 min
http_status — HTTP response classes counted from the traffic log FortiWeb 5 min
infra — the VM and its hypervisor host (CPU, memory, disk, network, load) FortiWeb, FortiADC — only when mapped 3 min
snmp — uptime, interfaces (state, byte counters), CPU / memory / disk over SNMP v2c every product — opt-in per appliance 3 min

Beyond the device APIs: SNMP polling and the syslog receiver

Every collector above reads the appliance's own REST or CLI. Two do not, and they are what a customer's monitoring already speaks:

  • snmp polls the appliance over SNMP v2c — sysUpTime, the interface table (operational state and the 64-bit byte counters, 32-bit on a build without ifXTable) and CPU / memory / disk from the vendor MIB (FortiWeb verified on 7.6.8; the other products' OIDs are the documented ones and fall back to HOST-RESOURCES when the agent lacks them). It is opt-in per appliance: open the appliance's edit form, switch on Poll this appliance over SNMP v2c, set the port (161) and the community string, which is stored like the passwords (encrypted, mirrored to the vault when one is configured) and never shown again. On the appliance, allow SNMP on the management interface and list this node — and its HA peer — as a query host. Switching it off disables the target instead of leaving a row that goes red. Series: satom_snmp_sysuptime_seconds, satom_snmp_if_oper_up, satom_snmp_if_in_octets_total / _out_octets_total (labels iface, ifindex), satom_snmp_cpu_pct, satom_snmp_mem_pct, satom_snmp_disk_pct; a failed poll writes satom_scrape_up{collector="snmp"} 0. SNMPv3 is not supported (no User Security Model yet; it arrives when a customer needs it), and SATOM sends no traps and receives none.
  • The syslog receiver takes the appliances' own event stream directly — UDP and TCP, RFC 3164 and RFC 5424 framing, the Fortinet key=value body with or without a header. It is off by default; the card on this page switches it on, sets the bind address and port (default 5514: port 514 needs a port redirect or CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE on satom-scheduler.service, which is a signed-release change, not a setting) and lists extra sender networks. Only known senders are kept — the appliances' management addresses, plus the extra networks under their own address; anything else is dropped and counted (satom_syslog_dropped_total{reason}). The listener runs inside the scheduler sidecar on the primary (never on a standby, never in the web workers); the page shows what the sidecar last journalled: state, counts per device, drops, and — in Global only — the last 500 messages with credential-shaped values blanked. Series: satom_syslog_messages_total (device, facility, severity), satom_syslog_up{device} (1 when a message arrived since the previous pass, 0 for silence, for every known appliance), satom_syslog_dropped_total{reason}, satom_syslog_receiver_up. Log bodies at scale stay with the FortiAnalyzer; flows (NetFlow/sFlow) and packet capture are out of scope and stated as such. On a FortiWeb, point config log syslog-policy (a server row with this node's address, the port and proto udp) at the node and enable config log syslogd with that policy — measured on 7.6.8: a server row changed while syslogd is already enabled is not picked up until syslogd is disabled and enabled again.
