Administrators see every script and every user's runs and saved runs there too.

Saved runs. On the same page, a set of values can be saved with a cron expression (§15; the next five fire times are previewed as you type). A saved run is pinned to the version it was created against: publishing a new version changes nothing for it, and the row offers move to vN, which checks the saved values against the new form first. Password values of a saved run are kept in the vault (<mount>/scripts-saved/<script>/<id>), never in the saved-run file, and each fire hands the runner a single-use wrapped copy; without a vault, a saved run cannot keep one. The scheduler fires saved runs on the primary. A fire missed by more than five minutes (scheduler not running) is skipped, not replayed. A saved run whose owner is deactivated, loses operations.scripts_run or loses access to the script is paused with the reason instead of running on their behalf. Each user keeps at most 50 saved runs.

How a run is contained. Runs are executed by satom-scripts.service, not by the web application. That runner has no database connection and no access to the SATOM encryption key; it reads the frozen files and writes the run record. Each script runs in the bubblewrap jail of §35.3 (own process, user and network namespaces, none of SATOM mounted). A queued run holds the form values in a private file on this node only; the runner rewrites it without them the moment it starts. On an HA pair satom-scripts.path must be enabled on both nodes. An update arms it on nodes installed before it existed.

What a run can use. The runner unit carries cgroup limits, so a script that allocates, forks or writes in a loop stops at them instead of taking memory, processes or disk from the database and the web service on the same node: MemoryMax=1G (a run that reaches it is ended at once — the kernel picks the script, never the runner, and its record says the memory limit stopped it), TasksMax=256, CPUQuota=200% with a low CPU and I/O weight, and a private /tmp that is a 512 MB memory filesystem — the run's work directory lives there, so no run can fill the disk. Inside the jail the root and /dev are read-only, a single file is at most 256 MB and the output is read as it arrives (twice the 64 KB shown is kept). At most 50 runs wait in the queue (a full queue is refused with that message) and run records are kept 30 days (3,000 at most); a queued or running record is never pruned. The unit has no systemd start limit (it starts once per queued run), and a file in the queue that is not a run request is moved to data/scripts/rejected/. A site that needs more raises the limits in a systemd drop-in (systemctl edit satom-scripts.service). The integration-hooks runner (satom-integrations.service) has the same limits.

23.5 Data stores

Python Studio → Data stores holds tables you define in the UI. A data store is a column list — name, label, type (text, number, boolean, date, json) and required — plus rows. Every row also has _id, _created_at, _updated_at and _by.

  • Rows are added, edited and deleted from the store's page (click a row to edit it), by hand or by apps. Every value is checked against its column's type on the way in, and a column that is not declared is refused rather than dropped — a typo in an app's mapping must not write an empty column.
  • Columns can be added, renamed, reordered, retyped and removed at any time. Nothing stored is ever deleted by that: a removed column comes back with its values if you add it again, and a retyped one is re-checked on the next write.
  • CSV: Export CSV writes every row (spreadsheet-safe: a cell that starts like a formula is prefixed with '). Import CSV appends rows from a file whose header names the columns; every line is checked before any is written, so a file with one bad line imports nothing.
  • Limits: 20,000 rows and 16 MiB per store, 128 KiB per row, 64 KiB per value, 40 columns, 200 stores per node. A query reads the whole store to filter it, so the size cap is what bounds one query. Two writers of the same store are serialised, so a limit cannot be passed by writing at the same moment.

No SQL and no DDL is reachable from these pages: rows are JSON documents in SATOM's own database, so a data store cannot reach any other table — and it replicates to the standby and travels in backups and clones like the rest of the configuration. Gated by studio.script_library.

23.6 Connections

Python Studio → Connections names an external system once, with its credential, for app steps to use.

Kind Settings Authentication
HTTP API Base URL, TLS verification (against the trust store), timeout none, basic (user + password), bearer token, API key in a named header, OAuth2 client credentials (client id + secret + token URL + scope)
PostgreSQL Host, port, database, user, TLS verification, timeout password
  • Every call stays under the base URL. A step's path is joined to it; an absolute URL, //, .. or a backslash in a path is refused, and redirects are returned as the answer, never followed. A step cannot set the Authorization header, the API-key header, Host or Cookie.
  • The secret (password, token, API key, client secret) is write-only: the page can replace or clear it and never shows it. It is kept in the vault, or encrypted with SATOM's key, by the vault mode (§26), and Settings → Vault → migrate / remove local copies covers it like the other secrets. It is redacted out of every error text.
  • Where a connection may point. SATOM resolves the host once and refuses it when ANY address it resolves to is a loopback address, link-local (cloud metadata lives at 169.254.169.254), multicast, unspecified, reserved, or an address of this node itself — the node's metrics store, cache and web server listen there without authentication. Internal addresses (10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x) are allowed: internal APIs and CMDBs are what connections are for. The request then goes to the address that was checked (the name stays the Host header and the TLS server name), so a DNS answer that changes in between changes nothing. The same check covers the OAuth2 token URL (https only) and a PostgreSQL host, and it runs on every call — an app step, a list field filled from an API when a form opens, the Test button and a script. A refusal reads "… resolves to …, a loopback address of this node; a connection never dials it".
  • PostgreSQL queries take %(name)s parameters and run in a READ ONLY transaction unless the step ticks Allow writes. The connection is always encrypted: with TLS verification on, the server certificate is checked against the trust store (verify-full); off, it is encrypted without the check (require). A server without TLS is refused — the password never travels in clear.
  • Changing where a connection points clears its secret. The stored secret belongs to the destination: the scheme, host and port of the base URL, the authentication, the API-key header, the token URL, the user and TLS verification (for PostgreSQL: host, port, database, user and TLS). Change any of them and the secret is cleared — the page says so — and must be typed again; otherwise anyone allowed to edit a connection could point it at a server of their own and press Test to receive the token. Renaming, the description, the timeout and the path under the same host keep it.
  • A credential that comes back is masked. An API that echoes the request (a debug endpoint, a hostile server) would return the token in its answer; every answer is masked before a step, a script or an operator sees it — the secret, the Authorization value, the Basic header's base64 form and an OAuth2 access token, also in their JSON-escaped spelling.
  • The other HA node is refused too, like this node: every address listed in data/ha_nodes.json. A path may not carry an encoded ., / or \ (%2e, %2f, %5c — the same climb, spelt to slip past the check), and the query string is re-encoded pair by pair.
  • One call has one deadline: twice the timeout plus 5 s, whatever a slow server does (a server that sends a byte at a time would otherwise hold a web worker as long as it liked).
  • PostgreSQL runs ONE statement (the extended protocol: SELECT 1; COMMIT; … is refused) and a read-only step is read-only twice — the transaction and the session default — so a statement list cannot walk out of it. A result stops at the row limit or at 8 MiB, the server stops a statement at the timeout and SATOM cancels it if it does not. With libpq 16 or later, a server that asks for the password in clear is refused before the password is sent. The real boundary stays a read-only role on the remote database: a function with side effects is still a single SELECT.
  • Test tries a GET (or a read-only SQL statement) and shows the answer; type a JSON path (a.b[0].c, items[*].name) to see what a step would keep.

Connections are called by SATOM, and the credential is never in a script's hands. App steps and the Test button call from the web server. A Script Library script may call the connections it declares (script editor → Settings → Connections):

from satom_script import connection, result

crm = connection("crm")
r = crm.get("/tickets", params={"state": "open"})      # also post/put/patch/delete
result(r.json())
rows = connection("cmdb").query("SELECT name FROM hosts WHERE site = %(s)s",
                                {"s": "zrh"})["rows"]   # read-only unless write=True

The script sends the request to the scripts runner, which adds the credential OUTSIDE the sandbox and returns the answer: the token, password or client secret is never in the script's environment, input or files. Only declared connections answer, whatever the script's network setting (a script with no outbound access can still use them), each call is a line in the run's connections log, and a secret that shows up in the output is masked. A connection with a secret needs the vault: the run receives a single-use wrapped token (like script credentials, §23.4), never the secret on disk. A published version keeps the connections it declared. A connection that a script declares cannot be deleted.

API Catalog: the versions of an API someone publishes

When a team (or a vendor) publishes an API you want to use, Python Studio → API Catalog keeps it, one entry per version of it — inventory 1.0, inventory 1.1, inventory 2.0.

  1. New API: an id, a name, the owner (who publishes it) and a link to its own documentation.
  2. Create draft on the API page: a version number, starting empty or from an earlier version.
  3. Fill the draft's endpoints: Import an OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 document (JSON or YAML, uploaded or pasted, up to 8 MiB), or Add endpoint by hand (id, method, path with {name} for a path parameter, summary, query parameters, whether it takes a body) — or import first and correct by hand. Only references inside the document are followed; nothing is downloaded. HEAD/OPTIONS operations are skipped, and an operationId that is missing, repeated or not usable is replaced by method_path (the import says so).
  4. Publish. A published version never changes and is never deleted; later changes go into a new version. Deprecate marks a version you want people to move off; it keeps working.

Compare two versions on the API page lists the endpoints removed (calls to them break), changed (method, path, parameters or body) and added. Endpoints (JSON) downloads a version's list in the shape the manual editor saves, to paste into another version or another SATOM.

Pin a connection to a version (HTTP connection page → API version; published versions only). From then on:

  • the Call an API app step offers the version's endpoints in an Endpoint picker; picking one sets the method and the path, and Path parameters (JSON, e.g. {"id": "{{ form.id }}"}) fill its {name} parts — each value percent-encoded into one segment;
  • a step that types a method and path must still name an endpoint of that version: otherwise it is a problem that blocks publishing the app, and it is refused when it runs, before anything reaches the network. A POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE endpoint is a write, so a rehearsal never sends it;
  • a script calls endpoints by id and only those:
from satom_script import connection, result

inv = connection("inventory")
host = inv.op("getHost", {"id": 7}).json()       # method and path from the catalog
hosts = inv.op("listHosts", params={"limit": 50}).json()
result({"api": inv.catalog()["version"], "endpoints": len(inv.operations())})

inv.get("/hosts") still works when GET /hosts is an endpoint of the version; a request that is not one is refused by the scripts runner. The script editor's Connections card shows the endpoints of every declared, pinned connection with the line to paste.

Moving a connection to another version names the app steps that call an endpoint the new version does not have, and saves only when you confirm; those apps then show the problem and cannot be published until it is fixed. A connection with no version keeps the old behaviour: any path under its base URL. An API with connections pinned to it cannot be deleted.

23.7 Apps

Python Studio → Apps builds a small application — a form, a diagram of steps and an output with actions — and publishes it as its own entry in Operations → Plugins (in the Global ADOM: Global → Plugins).

The editor has six tabs:

  • Settings — name and icon of the menu entry, description, where it appears (the ADOMs you tick, or every ADOM) and who may use it (the groups and the people you tick; every Python Studio author can too). Nobody else sees the entry or can open the app, its runs or their actions.
  • Form — the fields the user fills in: text, textarea, number, date, checkbox, password and three lists — a fixed list, a list from a data store column (value and label columns) and a list from an API (a connection, a path, the JSON path of the list and the value / label keys). The value chosen must be one of the choices the server reads again.
  • Diagram — the same editor as Process. Steps: Start, End, Set a variable, Decision (equals, not equals, contains, greater, less, empty, not empty, true → yes / no), Fail (stop with a message), Output (a value shown as a table, list, key/value, text or JSON), Read a data store, Write a data store (insert, update, upsert, delete), Query a database, Call an API (with Keep only (JSON path)) and Run a script (the published version of a Script Library script, with its form values). A step saves its result under a name (Save the result as).
  • Actions — buttons under the output of a finished run: Save to a data store, Download (CSV or JSON), Send to a connection, Run another app with the output, Raise a change request. Each can ask for confirmation.
  • Test — runs the saved draft, as a rehearsal by default: steps that write (data store writes, SQL with writes allowed, API calls other than GET) are described, not executed.
  • Publish — lists what must be fixed first, freezes the draft as version N, and Unpublish removes the entry from the menu.

Templates. Text parameters are templates rendered in a sandbox: {{ form.host }}, {{ rows }}, {{ rows | length }}, {{ response.items[0].id }}. A value that is exactly one {{ expression }} keeps its type, so a query result reaches a script or an output as a list, not as text. An undefined name is an error the run shows; write {{ x | default('') }} for an optional one. JSON parameters (filters, values, bodies) are JSON whose strings are templates.

Arrows. A step ends ok or error; a decision ends yes or no. The run follows the arrow of that outcome, otherwise the always arrow — except after an error: an error follows only an error arrow, and with none the run stops there as failed (the message is in {{ last_error }} on an error path). A loop is allowed and stops after 200 steps; a run stops after 10 minutes.

Running. The user fills in the form and presses Run; the run continues in the background and the page follows it, then shows the outputs, the actions and the steps. Password values are masked in every run record. Each user sees their own runs; authors see all of them and the run's variables.

Actions and devices. Raise a change request never changes a device: it creates a draft change request (title, reason, change type, device ids, risk, with the app and run named in it) that goes through the normal approval of Change Management. Run another app needs the user to be allowed to use that app.

Limits that protect the node. App runs execute in the web service, so:

  • a user has at most 2 runs in progress and the node at most 8; the Run button is also limited to 30 presses a minute, and a run request larger than 1 MiB is refused (413);
  • a template cannot compute without end: ** refuses an exponent above 64, * refuses a result longer than 1 MiB, all the range() loops of one value together produce at most 1,000,000 items, and a rendered text stops at 1 MiB;
  • a value a template puts into an API path is percent-encoded, slash included: a form value such as 1?admin=1 or ../../users stays one path segment instead of becoming a query or a climb (to pass values as query parameters, use the step's Query string (JSON));
  • a list filled from an API is fetched at most once a minute, not on every form opening;
  • an action runs once per run (Download can be repeated), and only on the version that produced the run: after a new Publish, an older run's actions are refused — run the app again;
  • users who are not authors see which steps ran and how they ended, not their details (a decision prints both values it compared, which may be data the app never chose to show); the message of a Fail step is shown;
  • password values are masked also in the spellings the usual filters produce (urlencode, tojson, base64);
  • run records are kept 90 days.

Gated by studio.script_library for authors; users need only to be in the app's access list.

23.8 Examples

Python Studio → Examples installs working examples of every Studio piece with one click. Ids start with ex-; installing creates only what is missing and never overwrites an object you edited; Remove deletes the objects of that example but keeps any of them something else still uses (another example's app, or your own work built on it). Connections are created without a secret and pointed at a placeholder host (fortigate.example.com, netbox.example.com), so nothing reaches a device until you open the connection, set the address and paste the token.

Example What it shows Objects
FortiGate: which rule lets this traffic through? An app built only from the diagram, three API calls and two decisions; actions on the output: save to a data store, download CSV, ask for the access as a change request. The same lookup as a script. connection ex-fortigate, data store ex-policy-lookups, script ex-fortigate-policy-lookup, app ex-policy-finder
NetBox: who owns this IP address? A script that calls a connection, and an app whose diagram runs that script. connection ex-netbox, script ex-netbox-ip-owner, app ex-ip-owner
Explain a flow (FortiGate + NetBox) One script, two connections: who owns both ends and which rule decides the flow. Keeps working when NetBox is down. script and app ex-traffic-explainer (+ the two connections)
Data stores: site contacts No external system: a list field fed by a data store, a query, an upsert. Published at once (every ADOM, Studio authors), so it appears under Operations → Plugins. data store ex-site-contacts (3 sample rows), apps ex-site-contact, ex-site-contact-edit

The Console pane has two examples in its Studio group: the fleet inventory printed as CSV (paste it into a data store's Import CSV) and every managed FortiGate with the base URL a connection to its REST API would use.

FortiGate setup. On the FortiGate: System → Administrators → Create New → REST API Admin, a read-only profile, this SATOM node as trusted host; copy the token. In SATOM open ex-fortigate: base URL https://<FortiGate>/api/v2, authentication Bearer, paste the token, Test with /monitor/system/status. With a self-signed certificate import its CA into the trust store (or untick TLS verification on a lab box).

The policy finder, step by step (ex-policy-finder, the answers are the ones a FortiGate 8.0.1 gives):

  1. Route back to the source — GET /monitor/router/lookup?destination=<source>, Keep only results.entries[0].interface → srcintf (e.g. port1). The ingress interface is the one the FortiGate uses to reach the source.
  2. Is there a route? — decision {{ srcintf | default('') }} not empty; no → Fail "The FortiGate has no route to …".
  3. Ask the FortiGate — GET /monitor/firewall/policy-lookup with query {"srcintf": "{{ srcintf }}", "sourceip": "{{ form.source }}", "dest": "{{ form.destination }}", "protocol": "{{ {'tcp': 6, 'udp': 17}[form.protocol] }}", "destport": "{{ form.port }}"}, keep results → verdict: {"match": true, "policy_id": 1, "policy_action": "accept"} or {"match": false, "policy_id": 0, "sec_default_action": "deny"}.
  4. Does a rule match? — decision {{ verdict.match }} true.
  5. Read the rule — GET /cmdb/firewall/policy/{{ verdict.policy_id }}, keep results[0] → rule (name, interfaces, addresses, services).
  6. Verdict — a Set a variable step builds one record with a dictionary expression, e.g. 'src_addr': rule.srcaddr | map(attribute='name') | join(', '); the deny branch builds the same record with policy_name "(no rule matches)".
  7. Show the verdict as key/value. Any API error follows the error arrow to Fail "The FortiGate did not answer: {{ last_error.message }}".

The same lookup as a Script Library script (ex-fortigate-policy-lookup):

from satom_script import connection, inputs, log, result

fgt = connection("ex-fortigate")          # SATOM adds the token; the script never sees it

def get(path, **params):
    r = fgt.get(path, params=params or None)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return (r.json() or {}).get("results")

src, dst = inputs["source"].strip(), inputs["destination"].strip()
ingress = get("/monitor/router/lookup", destination=src)["entries"][0]["interface"]
lookup = get("/monitor/firewall/policy-lookup", srcintf=ingress, sourceip=src, dest=dst,
             protocol="6", destport=str(inputs["port"]))
if lookup.get("match"):
    rule = get("/cmdb/firewall/policy/%d" % lookup["policy_id"],
               format="policyid|name|srcaddr|dstaddr|service|action")[0]
    result({"policy": rule["name"], "action": lookup["policy_action"]})
else:
    result({"policy": None, "action": lookup.get("sec_default_action", "deny")})

NetBox setup. In NetBox create a read-only API token. In SATOM open ex-netbox: base URL https://<NetBox>/api, authentication API key, header Authorization, secret Token <key> (a v1 token; with a v2 token, NetBox 4.5+, choose Bearer and paste the token alone). Test with /status/. The script reads /ipam/ip-addresses/?address=<ip> (status, DNS name, tenant, the device or virtual machine and interface it is assigned to) and /ipam/prefixes/?contains=<ip>, sorted most specific first (VLAN, role, scope, tenant):

from satom_script import connection, inputs, result
nb = connection("ex-netbox")
ip = inputs["ip"]
addr = nb.get("/ipam/ip-addresses/", params={"address": ip}).raise_for_status().json()
nets = nb.get("/ipam/prefixes/", params={"contains": ip}).raise_for_status().json()
result({"records": addr["results"], "prefixes": [p["prefix"] for p in nets["results"]]})

The ex-ip-owner app runs that script with a Run a script step ({"ip": "{{ form.ip }}"} → nb), then shows {{ nb.owner }} as key/value and {{ nb.prefixes }} as a table, or a text when NetBox does not know the address.

Data stores, step by step (ex-site-contact-edit): a Write a data store step in upsert mode with match {"site": "{{ form.site }}"} and values {"site": "{{ form.site }}", "contact": "{{ form.contact }}", …} updates the row of that site or inserts it; a Read a data store step with filter {"site": "{{ form.site }}"} reads it back. The ex-site-contact form's Site field is a list from the data store (value and label column site), so a site added by the edit app appears in it.

23.9 What Studio code cannot do to SATOM

The rules below were checked by a security review and an adversarial test on a running node (2026-10-20); each one is pinned by a test (tests/test_studio_security.py).

Property What protects it
Confidentiality of SATOM Scripts and the console run in a bubblewrap jail with none of SATOM mounted (no .env, database socket, keys or other processes); the scripts runner itself has no database and no encryption key. Connection secrets reach a run only as single-use vault tokens unwrapped outside the jail. A connection never dials this node, the other HA node, loopback, link-local or reserved addresses. A connection's secret is cleared when its destination changes, and an echoed credential is masked in every answer. Operators see an app's outputs, not its step details.
Integrity of SATOM No SQL or DDL reaches SATOM's database from Studio: data stores are checked JSON rows. Device changes from an app are draft change requests that wait for approval. A PostgreSQL step runs one statement, read-only unless allowed. Path values cannot leave their segment. Actions run once per run, on the version that produced it.
Availability of SATOM The scripts and hooks runners have cgroup limits (memory 1 GiB, 256 tasks, 2 CPUs, a 512 MB memory /tmp); the jail's root and /dev are read-only and its output is read with a cap. The console has no writable path, 512 MiB per process, a task headroom and one run at a time. App runs are capped per user and per node, templates are bounded, HTTP calls have one total deadline, query results stop at 8 MiB, data stores have row, size and count limits, the scripts queue holds at most 50 runs, and request bodies to the app and Studio pages are capped.

What stays the administrator's responsibility: a Studio author (studio.script_library) writes code and diagrams that run with the connections' credentials, so grant that key as you would an administrator's; use read-only credentials on the external systems (a REST API admin with a read-only profile, a read-only database role) wherever a script or app only reads.

24. High availability

Settings → System → High Availability (admin, user_manage). This page was split out of Software Update so that the two questions get their own nav entry: Software Update (§22) is "what code is this node running"; High Availability is "how many nodes are there, which one is primary, and is the standby actually receiving anything".

Loading it never touches an appliance. Everything on it comes from this node's own PostgreSQL plus a best-effort HTTP probe of the peer, so the page opens with the entire fleet switched off.

Cluster architecture graph. One card per registered node, laid out with the live replication arrow drawn between them: role (primary / standby), host, reachability, revision, health. Click a node to load it into the editor below. The arrow's direction is the real streaming direction and its label carries the current WAL lag — the reconciler drives the staged code rollout along that same path. Below the graph is a fixed reference table of the node-to-node channels and what each carries, which exists because :443 (your browser → the app) is routinely confused with the node-to-node traffic; the heavy sync — the standby's actual database — is Postgres streaming replication, not the peer HTTPS channel. Live per-channel encryption status is on Monitoring → SATOM health (§14.1).

Deployment mode. A switch between HA and STANDALONE. It lives in the replicated settings table, which means it can only be written where Postgres is read-write: the primary. On a standby the page says so instead of failing the save. (The related deploy automation switch — reconciler AUTO vs MANUAL — is on the Software Update page, because it is about how code rolls out.)

The HA node registry. Add / update / remove the peer by name (its hostname) and host. The registry is a file in the replicated data directory: it reaches the peer on the next data sync, and its live state is probed on this page rather than trusted from the record. You cannot remove the node you are on.

Database replication & failover. The card shows the live streaming state read from the local PostgreSQL — on a primary the sender side (who is connected, in what state, how many bytes behind), on a standby its own apply lag.

Manual failover is guarded three ways. Promote this node to PRIMARY only appears on a node that is genuinely in recovery; it requires typing that node's hostname exactly; and it does not run in the web worker — it enqueues, and a privileged runner performs the promotion. Promote only when the old primary is confirmed down: nothing in SATOM arbitrates a split brain for you. On the primary the card says plainly that failover is initiated from the standby's own page.

Further reading — neither of these is a page in the product, and both matter the day something goes wrong:

  • Encryption in transit, node TLS & the service certificate — what each channel encrypts, and how the node's own certificate is issued and renewed (the settings for it are §26.8).
  • Git backup and surviving a Gitea outage — what keeps working when the code remote is unreachable, and how to recover from it.
  • Running SATOM in containers — the third installation shape, whose cluster this page does not describe: there the standby is a PostgreSQL streaming replica whose scheduler idles until promotion, the reverse proxy carries it as backup rather than as the other half of a balancer, and promotion is an operator decision the stack deliberately refuses to undo for you.

24.1 The HA link — when the standby stops taking code from the primary

The standby gets new code by running git fetch against the primary's repository over SSH, as the service account (its reconciler does it every minute). That one channel can fail while everything else stays green: root SSH, the data/ sync, replication and both web UIs keep working.

What it looked like (2026-10-11). systemd-logind on the primary lost a job (Failed to start session scope session-NNNN.scope: Connection timed out). From then on every SSH login of the service account stayed in logind state opening: sshd waits on pam_systemd and never runs the command, so every fetch hung for 120 s and the standby silently stopped converging. The fix was systemctl restart systemd-logind on the primary; the standby caught up within one reconciler cycle.

Where you see it now.

  • Software Update & HA on the primary has an HA link card. It shows the standby's own account of itself — in sync, N commits behind, or cannot fetch from this node since : — plus this node's systemd-logind (logins of the service account stuck in opening for more than 60 s, or a loginctl that does not answer) and whether sshd answers. The standby's state comes from its /healthz/reconciler probe (the same peer-probe pattern as /healthz/backups; it publishes the decision, the commit counts, short shas, the time and a one-line redacted error — nothing else). These probes answer only a request signed with the inter-node identity key (HMAC over the request with a ±120 s timestamp window, so both nodes' clocks must be NTP-synchronised; the key itself never crosses the wire); anyone else gets 403, and plain /healthz gives them ok and nothing more. A pair without an identity key therefore shows its peer as unreachable on these pages. The lag is computed on the primary against its own branch head, because a standby that cannot fetch measures itself against a stale origin and would read "0 behind".
  • Each node's reconciler status is node-local (state/reconciler-status.json, outside data/). It used to live in data/, which the data sync overwrites with the primary's copy every five minutes, so the standby's file always named the primary. A fetch timeout is now recorded as a fetch-error decision with the error and how long the streak has lasted, instead of an exception in the journal.
  • The Deploy automation card on each node's Software Update & HA page shows this node's own last reconciler tick, read from that file — on the standby that is the standby's own decision, including cannot fetch since (N failed attempts in a row): . The record the primary publishes into the replicated settings is shown below it, labelled Primary's reconciler, only on a node it does not describe.
  • A code update (and its rollback) now restarts satom-reconciler along with the scheduler (try-restart: a stopped reconciler stays stopped). Before, the loop kept running the release it was started with — on 2026-10-11 the standby's had been up since the morning on code older than its tree. Until a node's reconciler has been restarted once on this release, it still writes its record to the old data/ path; the page reads that as a fallback, but only when the record names this node.
  • The alert engine (Settings → Alerts, git family) raises HA link broken when the standby has been failing to fetch for more than 10 minutes or this node's login path is wedged — once per incident: it re-arms only after the link has been seen healthy again.
  • satom ha check on the primary prints the same check in the console (satom show runbook ha-link is the offline procedure).

Repairing it. Repair HA link… on the card (admin, user_manage), or sudo satom ha repair on the primary. Both first show a preview — the current check, what the repair does and what it does not — and change nothing until you confirm (the button) or add --yes (the CLI). Confirmed, it:

  • restarts systemd-logind on the primary — not from the web worker, but by enqueuing an allowlisted request for the privileged runner, the same queue as every Settings → Services action (logind is restart-only there and is not drawn on the Services card);
  • follows the runner's steps, then re-runs the check and shows before and after;
  • is written to the audit log (ha.link.repair, or ha.link.repair.refused).

It does not touch the standby or anything over SSH, restart sshd, the web app, PostgreSQL or the data sync, or end open sessions (logind re-attaches them). It cannot fix a dead sshd, an unreachable standby or a refused key — the check names those separately (sshd-down, standby-unreachable) so the button is not pressed for the wrong fault. It refuses on a standby or a standalone node and says why: the login service on the fetch path is the primary's. The runner re-checks the role against its own PostgreSQL as well.

Manual fallback, if the app itself cannot run the check:

loginctl list-sessions
loginctl show-session <id> -p Name -p State -p Timestamp   # 'opening' for minutes = wedged
journalctl -u systemd-logind --since -2h | grep -i 'session scope'
sudo systemctl restart systemd-logind
# on the standby, read-only: is it fetching again?
journalctl -u satom-reconciler -n 20

25. AppIDs

Global ADOM → Administrator → AppIDs (admin, user_manage).

An AppID is two things at once, which is why it has its own catalog rather than living in a policy comment:

  • a billing key — which customer a FortiWeb Server Policy is charged to;
  • an access-control unit — the scope an API token can be pinned to, so an external integrator only reaches the backends of their AppIDs.

Because it decides money and permissions, the authority is always the two local tables — the catalog and the policy bindings — never a file and never a comment string. Files and URLs are sources that feed the catalog.

Manual vs imported, and the stale badge. A row you type by hand is a manual entry. A row that arrived from a feed is imported. Import is strictly additive: it inserts, updates and stamps last_seen. An imported AppID that stops appearing in the feed is flagged stale for review — it is never deleted and never unassigned, because that would silently de-bill a customer or drop a token's scope. Manual rows are never auto-staled.

The upload flow — map once, reuse forever.

  1. Upload a CSV, TSV, TXT or PDF. The file is parsed and previewed; nothing is imported yet.
  2. Map the columns to the fields: app_id (required), plus customer, label and rate, and any number of extra named columns you want carried along. Column references are header names, or index numbers if you say the file has no header row.
  3. Import. The mapping is saved, and it is reused by every later upload and by the nightly scheduled action — that is the whole point. You map once, not once per file.

External source (for the nightly). Configure a URL, its auth mode (none / basic / bearer) and the credential; the secret is stored Fernet-encrypted and is never returned to the browser (the page only tells you whether one is set). The scheduled action appid_import (§15) fetches that URL, applies the saved mapping and imports additively. With no source configured the nightly reports "no source configured" rather than pretending it ran.

Assignment. Assign an AppID to a Server Policy by picking the device and the policy name. The binding is unique per (appliance, server policy), so a policy belongs to exactly one AppID; assigning a second one replaces the first rather than double-billing. Unassign is a separate action. Deleting an AppID also deletes its bindings, and says so.

The assignment picker spans both FortiWeb and FortiADC appliances — the catalog is a single global one, not per-ADOM.

26. Settings, tab by tab

Settings is one page with a grouped sidebar: 11 groups, 40 panels. Ten of the groups (38 panels) are admin-only (user_manage); the remaining one — My Account, holding Security and Change Password — is self-service and is the only group a non-admin sees. A group with nothing you may see is not rendered at all, so the menu never offers a section that is not there.

Group Panels
System General · Software Update Repository · Software Update · High Availability · System Automations · Scout · Integrations
Source of Truth & Backup Configuration SoT · Backup Server · System Backup & Restore · Deploy Clone
Access & Identity Users · Profiles · Authentication · Access Control · Vault
Certificates & Trust Certificate Manager · Node TLS · Trust store
Network & DNS DNS Lookup · DNS Records
Fleet & Devices Hypervisors · ADOMs · Policy Links · Clone / Migrate
User Interface Appearance · Languages · ADOM Menus
My Account Security · Change Password
Monitoring & Alerts Email & Alerts · Thresholds
Sentinel Settings · Context · Response policy · Border blocklist · Architecture · Incidents console
Path Diagnostics Settings · Architecture

The Scout panel (the AI assistant, §33) additionally needs advisor.configure; an admin without it does not see the entry. Sentinel and Path Diagnostics settings are admin-only end to end: saving them (including Path Diagnostics's site-wide on/off switch) needs Manage users, the same as seeing the panes. Sentinel's AI reasoning ships with an empty model endpoint and stays off until one is set (for example http://localhost:11434), even if its switch is on.

Integrations is a page, not a pane, and its row carries the leaving arrow (↗) for that reason: clicking it replaces the console instead of switching a tab. It is where SATOM is wired to systems it does not own — NetBox (maintenance windows and the appliance → device map) and your own Python hooks — and it is filed under System because that is what it configures. It had no menu entry at all until 2026-09-21; the page existed and worked, but the only way to reach it was to type /settings/integrations.

Software Update, High Availability, System Automations and System Backup & Restore are pages too (↗), filed in Settings (until 3.4.4 they were under Administrator → System). Each keeps its own address and draws this menu with itself selected. System Backup & Restore sits with the backup surfaces; the other three under System. System Automations keeps the ADOM you are in: its list shows that ADOM's rows, as before.

Deploy Clone copies a whole installation's data into this one, or exports this one for another (§11.1). It sits in Source of Truth & Backup because it moves the same estate the backup bundles carry. It is not Clone / Migrate under Fleet & Devices, which copies configuration from one appliance to another.

Path Diagnostics is its own group, below Sentinel. Its Settings panel holds only where to look and how long to wait — the default look-back window, the FortiAnalyzer ADOM and device selector the border rung queries, the two timeouts. What a verdict means is on the same panel as a read-only table: the dominant-phase share and floor, the signals that count as an appliance being unfit to serve, the order conflicting border rows are resolved in, and the methods Path Diagnostics is permitted to send. Those are shown rather than offered on purpose — editing a threshold makes whoever changed it a second author of every report already filed, and an archived report says nothing about the values in force when it was written. Each row names the symbol it is read from, and the values are read off the engine when the page renders, so the table cannot drift from the code. Architecture renders the ten rungs from the same tuple the engine walks.

A typed Published host follows the free-target rule. Left blank, Path Diagnostics dials the object's VIP as the device reports it. A host you type is dialled only if the appliance publishes it — its own address on its management or SSH port, or one of its published services on that service's own port — unless you hold monitoring.probe_free or user management — the same rule as the certificate inspector and the transaction tracer.

Three repositories-or-destinations, three separate entries. Until 2026-08-29 the System group carried one panel called SoT & Backup, and it held a firmware git URL, the SFTP credentials of the backup box and nothing about appliance configuration at all — under a heading whose first word names an authority. Reading it as covering all three was the obvious reading and the wrong one. They are now three entries in two groups, and each states what it is not:

Entry What it is What it is not
Configuration SoT (§26.5) the versioned, hashed history of every appliance's configuration not firmware, not backups, not code
Backup Server (§26.5b) an SFTP destination three streams are copied to not an authority — nothing is consulted there to decide what a device is configured to do
Software Update Repository (§26.4) the git repo this node downloads its own code from has never held a device configuration or a firmware image

Firmware is not a source of truth in this product, and no panel offers a setting that says it is. Its authority is the firmware_images table plus data/firmware/, on Infrastructure → Firmware (§20), which is indexed, hashed and inside every backup bundle. The retired sot.firmware_repo_url / sot.firmware_repo_branch settings pointed at a second git repo holding a firmware manifest; every consumer of them merely printed the URL, nothing ever read the manifest, and the repo they named declared firmwares: [] while two images were loaded on the node. A setting that announces an authority nobody reads is worse than no setting, so it was removed rather than filled in.

Sentinel is its own group, and all six of its entries are panes. They are ordered by what they are, not by when they arrived: the four configuration surfaces first, then the reference document, then the live console. The Border blocklist sits last of the four because it is the one that is read by something outside this product.

Settings holds the whole section inline — the pipeline stage by stage, the live weight table, the ten runnable demonstrations and the form. Context is trusted sources, maintenance windows, the appliance ↔ VM ↔ host topology map and the local CVE mirror; it looks like reference data and is not, because a trusted source is worth −35 points, the largest single weight in the whole scoring table, and it is the only thing that tells an authorised scan apart from an intrusion — the two produce a byte-for-byte identical attack log. Response policy is per-action autonomy and the four operating modes that preset it — Alert only, Alert and block, High, Ultra high, plus Custom, which is what the page reads the moment any of their values is edited by hand. A mode is a named set of values for knobs that already existed and nothing in the engine ever asks which one is active, so the name cannot describe behaviour the table below it does not have. Architecture renders the same document served at /sentinel/docs, and Incidents console the same live console served at /sentinel/ — health tiles, the seven-day figures and the incident table included.

Nothing in the group leaves the Admin Console, so none of the five is marked as doing so: every form returns to the pane it was fired from, and the status filter reloads Settings rather than jumping to /sentinel/. Opening one incident does leave, because an incident is a page of its own.

The incidents console no longer carries its own Architecture and Context buttons. They were removed at the same moment those two became menu entries, and only for that reason: until then the Context button was the only way to reach the page, so deleting it on its own would have removed the function rather than a duplicate.

Both standalone URLs are still there and unchanged — they are what the top navigation, the manual's links and the concept map use — and each is rendered from the same file as its pane, so the two surfaces cannot drift apart. The two configure-once groups sit at the bottom, in this order: Monitoring & Alerts, then Sentinel last.

The menu itself is defined once, in app/templates/settings/_nav.html, and every Settings surface includes that one file — the console and the standalone /settings/sentinel page alike. So the submenu no longer disappears when a deep link or a save redirect lands you on a standalone page, and an entry added or renamed changes on every surface at the same moment. On a standalone page the entries navigate back into the console (/settings/#tab-users) instead of switching a pane, because the panes are not on that page: a tab button there would be a row that highlights and then does nothing.

Regrouping the strip into a menu did not rename the panels' targets (#tab-auth and its siblings), so every deep link, every saved URL hash and every §26.x reference in this manual still lands exactly where it did. Throughout this manual a setting is addressed as Settings → <Panel>.

Seven tabs are documented where the feature they configure is documented, because the setting is meaningless without it. They are not repeated here:

Tab Documented in
Thresholds §14.10 — measurement policy for every probe and device roll-up
Trust store §10.1 — the CAs SATOM itself trusts when it dials an appliance
Certificate Manager §10 — issuance protocol, lifecycle policy, and the ACME provider registry
Hypervisors §21.1 — the Proxmox / ESXi endpoints provisioning may build on
Clone / Migrate §6 — dummy-VIP rewrite rules and the copy-WPP default
Appearance §19 — themes, tokens, logo and favicon
Sentinel Settings → Sentinel → Settings — every knob next to the pipeline it configures, the live scoring weights, and ten demonstrations runnable against the real engine, all rendered in the pane itself. The same section is also served standalone at /settings/sentinel — with the Admin Console submenu still beside it — which is where deep links and the save redirect from outside the console land. Context, Response policy, Architecture and Incidents console are panes beside it, rendered from the same files as /sentinel/context, /sentinel/policies, /sentinel/docs and /sentinel/. The incidents console's own Architecture and Context buttons went away in the same change that made those two menu entries — a duplicate control, not a door. Every element of that pane — each knob, each group heading, each of the four health chips and each link out — carries a ?; hovering it (or focusing it, or tapping it) opens the explanation of what the control does, where the code reads it and what breaks at either extreme. That text lives in the same catalog the form is generated from, so it cannot drift from the control it describes.

The rest follow.

26.1 General — identity, logging, and the Libraries panel

Application name (browser title and top bar), environment (which drives the PROD/DEV badge), default appliance platform, display timezone, and:

  • Session Lock (minutes) — an idle timeout (5 to 1440, default 60). A browser session with no activity for that long is signed out on its next request, with the message "Your session was locked after N minutes of inactivity." (script callers get a JSON 401). Page loads, navigation and every form or button that changes something count as activity; background refreshes — the notification bell, job progress, status badges, edit-lock heartbeats and other timed panel reloads — do not, so a tab left open still locks. API tokens are not affected. The lock is audited as session.idle_lock.
  • Log Levels and Log Format — which severities are written to the application log file and how (plain, detailed, or JSON lines). Applied at start-up and immediately on save.

The status-poll interval and raw-JSON toggle that used to sit here were removed: nothing ever read them. A separate card opts an admin in or out of bug-report notifications (bell + email).

The System Information card is read-only inventory — version, node, Python, and the library list. Underneath it sits Libraries, which is a second, separate updater and is easy to confuse with §22:

  • §22 Software Update moves the application code (a git revision, or a signed offline package).
  • Settings → General → Libraries moves the Python dependencies — one package at a time, from a curated allowlist, with a rollback point recorded per package.

They are different mechanisms with different blast radii, and they are deliberately not merged. Practical notes:

  • "Check for updates" is the only thing that reaches the package index, and it does so outside the page render — the Settings page itself never touches the network, so an unreachable index cannot hang or 500 it. Results are cached for hours; the button forces a fresh look. The status line names the source (pypi.org, or the index set in Update sources). A package the index did not answer for shows not checked, never a green tick.
  • Where the versions come from. By default the check asks https://pypi.org, and an Upgrade or Rollback runs pip in the node's virtual environment (/opt/satom/venv) for that one pinned version against pip's configured index (pypi.org, unless the node has its own pip configuration). With an index set in Update sources (below), both the check and the install use that index, and the job log shows a package index step naming it.
  • On an offline (air-gapped) node pypi.org is not reachable, so the card says versions were NOT checked and offers no Upgrade. That is expected: there, the libraries move with the signed update package (§22, Software Update & HA), unless an internal index is reachable and set in Update sources. Each package carries the wheels for the release's requirements.txt and installs them strictly offline (--no-index), so applying it brings every library to the version that release pins.
  • The web worker never runs pip. It writes a request that the privileged updater applies, and the allowlist is enforced in both places. A package that is not on the list is refused before it reaches the queue.
  • It is node-local by default. The virtual environment does not replicate. The card prints which node you are on. Ticking also the peer sends the same change to the other node, but only after it succeeded on this one: the two nodes never restart together, so a bad version takes down one node for the length of its auto-rollback, not the pair. If the change fails or rolls back here, the peer is left untouched and the job says so.
  • Extras are kept. A package pinned with extras in requirements.txt (psycopg[binary]) is installed, rolled back and re-pinned with them, so its companion package moves in lockstep.
  • Each change is a job on the server. It appears in the job dock and the Job Manager with the steps of both nodes. satom-scheduler drives it, not the browser, so you can close the page and the peer step still happens. The job survives the restarts the change itself causes. It ends as an error, naming the node, if either node fails or rolls back, if the peer refuses or cannot be reached, or if the updater never picks the request up. Reopening Settings shows a change that is still running. While the web restarts, the card shows "reconnecting…" rather than a failure.

System packages, under Libraries, is the same mechanism for the operating-system packages SATOM depends on. Today the list holds one: bubblewrap, the sandbox for operator Python (integration hooks, the Python console, Script Library). Without it that code is refused, never run unconfined. The sandbox mounts only /usr plus /bin, /sbin, /lib and /lib64 exactly as the host has them, so it works on usr-merged systems (Debian 12, RHEL 9) and on SLES / openSUSE Leap 15, where those are real directories. All of them are mounted read-only.

  • One column per registered node. ok means the package is installed and the sandbox actually works for the service account. installed, not usable means the binary is there but the kernel will not let the service account create namespaces (for example an LXC without user namespaces); the message says why. A node that did not answer shows unreachable, never ok.
  • Install appears while any node is not ok. It asks whether to install on every node or only this one. The privileged updater on each node picks the distribution's package manager, installs the package and runs the same sandbox check before it reports success. Like a Libraries change, it is a job on the server: the peer is asked only after this node succeeded, the two nodes never change at the same moment, and closing the page does not stop it.
  • The list is curated and install-only. The web worker sends a package key, never a package name or a command, and nothing here removes a package.
  • New installs bring bubblewrap with them (online and offline bundles). This card is how a node installed before that gets it.

Update sources, under System Information, says where this installation looks for updates. There are two sources, and each is set on its own: leave either on Default, or point one or both at an internal pipeline or mirror.

Source Default What reads it
Update packages the public feed (satom-system-upgrades/latest.json), or SATOM_UPGRADE_FEED when the node's environment sets it Software Update & HA: Check for a newer package online and Download & stage (§22)
Python libraries https://pypi.org/simple the Libraries card's Check for updates, every Upgrade / Rollback, and the dependency step of an update from the repository (§22)
  • A custom source is an https:// URL. For update packages it is the URL of a latest.json in the same format as the public one. Each release publishes it under a link that never changes, https://github.com/visionebc/SATOM/releases/latest/download/satom-update-latest.json. Behind a proxy repository of GitHub (a Nexus or Artifactory raw proxy of https://github.com/), use the same path under the mirror, https://<mirror>/visionebc/SATOM/releases/latest/download/satom-update-latest.json: the package is then downloaded through the mirror as well, and Test names it. A Docker registry proxy (of ghcr.io, for example) is not a GitHub mirror and cannot be used. For libraries it is a pip "simple" index, the URL you would give pip as --index-url: Nexus, Artifactory, devpi, a GitLab or Gitea package registry, or pypi.org itself. It covers the Python (pip) libraries only: operating-system packages (apt, zypper, dnf, including the System packages card) keep coming from the operating system's own repositories.
  • Authentication is None (a public URL) or User + token (HTTP Basic). For a service that only issues tokens, use the user name its documentation gives for token access (for example __token__ on PyPI-compatible registries).
  • Test reaches the source the form describes, saved or not, and says what it offers: the version the feed names, or the newest Flask on the index. Save stores it. A blank token field keeps the stored token.
  • The token is write-only. It is stored like every other credential, in the vault when one is configured (updates/feed, updates/index) and encrypted locally otherwise. It is never sent back to the page or written to the audit log. It goes only to the URL's own host and never follows a redirect, so a feed whose package lives on a CDN does not hand the CDN your token. pip gets it through its environment, never on a command line, and it is masked in every log line.
  • A source that cannot be used is refused, not replaced. If a source is set but its token cannot be read (the vault is sealed, or the key changed), the check, the download and the library change all stop with that reason. None of them quietly falls back to the public default. An update from the repository is the exception, on purpose: it is not stopped over its dependency step, which changes nothing unless requirements.txt changed. Its log has a package index step that names the index used, or says why pip used its own default: a warning when the configured index could not be read, or a note when the update came from the standby's reconciler, which does not read the settings.
  • Trust does not change with the source. An update package from an internal pipeline is verified against this node's trust store exactly like one from the public feed. A pipeline that republishes the signed packages works as is. One that builds its own packages needs its signing key added with satom execute trust add-key, as a deliberate decision.
  • Both nodes of an HA pair use the same sources: the settings replicate with the database.

26.1b Services — starting, stopping and restarting this node's units

The Services card at the bottom of the tab controls the units this node runs: the web app, the scheduler, the reconciler, the metrics store, the alert / certificate-renewal / data-sync timers, nginx and PostgreSQL. It is the same mechanism as Libraries above — the web worker never runs systemctl itself, and is deliberately not granted it, because a general systemctl permission reaches every unit on the machine and is therefore root by another name. Each click is queued for the privileged updater, which applies it and then re-reads the unit's state: a zero exit code from systemctl means the job was accepted, not that the daemon came up.

What you can do to each unit is a fixed table, and three restrictions in it are deliberate:

  • The updater itself is not listed. It is the component that applies these requests. Stopping it would mean no later request could be processed — including the one that would start it again.
  • The web app, nginx and PostgreSQL cannot be stopped from here, only restarted. Stopping any of them leaves recovery possible only from a shell, and this page exists for the operator who has the browser and not the shell.
  • Nothing is enabled or disabled. Start and stop are runtime-only, so a unit you stop here comes back at the next boot. The At boot column shows what the node arms, so that is visible rather than surprising. Changing it is a durable decision and stays with the installer and the CLI (§20).

Three practical notes:

  • Restarting the web app is safe to click. It kills the worker handling your click, so the page cannot report the result directly — instead the privileged runner keeps writing the log while the app is down, and the panel reconnects and shows you how it ended, health check included. Expect a few seconds where the console is unresponsive.
  • Restarting PostgreSQL bounces the cluster; a standby reconnects its replication stream on its own. If the app is left holding dead pooled connections the runner recycles the workers for you rather than leaving you a 500 with no obvious cause.
  • It acts on this node only. systemd is node-local; a peer is never touched from here. The card prints which node and role you are on. A unit that is not installed on this node — satom-ha-datasync.timer on a primary or a standalone install — is shown greyed with no buttons, not as a failure.

26.2 Access Control — who may reach the app at all

One gate here, and it is empty-means-everywhere:

  • IP whitelist — only these source addresses or CIDRs may reach the app. Leave it empty to allow all. Each entry is validated as an IP or CIDR on save and an invalid one is skipped with a warning rather than silently stored.

Loopback and admins are always allowed, on purpose: this page is exactly where a typo would otherwise lock everybody — including you — out of a running appliance.

There is no per-username allowlist. It was removed: three gates already answer "who may sign in", each in the place that owns the decision — the directory group filter (who may authenticate at all, §26.7), Require administrator approval (a first-time directory user lands disabled), and the profile (what they may do once inside, §26.3). A fourth list of names enforced nothing the other three did not and went stale on every import: an approved, enabled user still took a blanket 403 on every page. The IP whitelist stays because it answers a different question — where a session may come from, not who. If your install stored a list, the page shows it, says it is no longer enforced, and offers a button to clear the dead row.

The per-user top-bar banner picker is not here and is not a login banner: it is a personal appearance preference, saved against your account, on your Profile page. Each ADOM can carry a different one.

26.3 Users and Profiles

Groups (Administrator → Access → Groups) are named sets of users, managed with Manage users. Python Studio apps are shared with groups or people (§23.7): add a colleague to a group and they get every app shared with it. A group an app is shared with cannot be deleted until it is removed from the app. The same groups limit who reads a Wiki article (§46.1); the Wiki articles column counts the articles naming each group. Deleting a group a Wiki article names is allowed and leaves that article closed (its author and the moderators only), never open to everyone.

Users is the account list — create, disable, delete, assign a profile, and per row: Reset password (local accounts only; 12 to 1024 characters), Clear 2FA (shown when the account has two-factor enabled) and Unlock (shown when the account has failed sign-ins or is locked out; it clears the counter and the lock and nothing else — a disabled account stays disabled). Every action needs Manage users and lands in the audit log. A profile that holds only View users sees the same list read-only, with no controls; the sidebar shows it a Users entry. The Admins counter counts the accounts that can manage both users and profiles.

Profiles is the one that matters for §1: the three named profiles (readonly, operator, admin) are seeded, not hard-coded. This page composes permission sets from the granular catalog — eleven areas (Monitoring, Web Protection, Network, Operations, Backups, API Registry, Audit Log, Appliances, Studio, Users, Profiles), each with its own view/edit/apply- style actions — and you can create your own profiles freely. The three seeded ones exist because they reproduce the legacy role behaviour exactly; they are a starting point, not the ceiling.

A custom profile gets exactly what its keys say. Pages that show device content (FortiWeb workspace and protection pages, exceptions, artifacts, FortiADC / FortiAnalyzer / FortiAuthenticator pages, the API registry, Sentinel, the network tools) need the matching view key, and the Global home lists appliances only with View appliances. The sidebar, the top bar and the home shortcuts offer a page only when the profile can open it, so a narrow profile sees a short menu rather than links that answer access denied.

An anti-lockout guard keeps at least one active account holding both user management and profile management, so this page cannot be used to remove the last administrator.

ADOMs. A profile can be confined to some ADOMs: tick them in the ADOMs card of the profile (no ADOM ticked = every ADOM, which is what every profile had before). A confined profile:

  • sees only its ADOMs in the switcher and the sidebar; opening any other ADOM — by link, URL or the X-ADOM header — is refused with Your profile does not include the … ADOM (a JSON caller gets 403);
  • sees, in the Global console, only the devices and records of its ADOMs: appliance lists and pages, jobs, change requests (one that also names a device outside its ADOMs is not shown), Sentinel incidents and border maps, certificates, reports, metrics and the dashboard tiles; a record it creates from Global lands in one of its ADOMs;
  • cannot open the database browser, the SQL console or DB reports (raw SQL reads every ADOM), nor ADOM Assets from Global (open it from one of its ADOMs). Script Library database fields still work: SATOM adds the ADOM filter to them (§23.4).

Background work (scheduled actions, sweeps already started, the scheduler) is not a session and acts on the whole fleet as before; a saved script run reads its database rows with its owner's ADOMs.

Nobody can grant more than they hold. A holder of Manage users or Manage profiles who is not a full administrator cannot assign or create a profile wider than their own, cannot reset the password or clear the 2FA of an account that holds more than they do, cannot add a key they do not hold to a profile, and cannot edit the profile they are assigned to. You may move yourself to a narrower profile, never a wider one. The same holds for ADOMs: a confined administrator composes and assigns profiles only within its own ADOMs and can never create or assign an unconfined one.

26.4 Software Update Repository — where this node downloads its own code from

This is the product's source code, and the only one of the three repositories-or-destinations above that a software update is pulled from. It is not where appliance configuration is versioned (§26.5) and not where backups are stored (§26.5b). The panel was labelled Git until 2026-08-29 — a tool name, which distinguished it from nothing.

  • Repository — remote, branch, HEAD, working-tree status and ahead/behind, refreshed on demand.

Which remote should be here? For an installation you did not build yourself, the answer is the public repository the installer clones by default, github.com/visionebc/SATOM. Development happens in a separate, private repository that a customer node is not expected to reach. Between 2026-07 and 2026-08-30 there was a third, intermediate mirror; it has been retired and deleted, so a node still pointing at it fails its next update with a 404 on a remote that no longer exists rather than with anything that names the real problem. If Repository shows a satom-prod URL, re-point it here before the next maintenance window. - Configure repository — set the remote URL, an optional token (embedded in the URL, never displayed back) and the branch. It is folded away behind the Edit button on the Repository card, and opens by itself on exactly one kind of node: one that has no origin at all, i.e. was never registered at installation. Such a node also says so, in as many words, above the form.

Until 2026-08-29 this was a second card of equal weight, permanently open, whose three boxes render empty until the status fetch fills them. A submit before that fetch lands writes blanks over a working remote. The repository is a fact to read; the form is only ever the answer on a fresh install, and that is the one state it now opens in. Whether a repository exists is decided server-side, on the first render — a client-side guess flashes the form open on a node that has been registered for a year. - Update from Gitea — a fast-forward-only git pull. Python changes need a service restart to take effect; the normal path for a code change is §22, not this button. - Manual git console — one git command per line, # for comments. It is git-only, not a shell: anything that is not a git subcommand is refused. - Recent commits lists what actually landed.

See also git backup and surviving a Gitea outage.

26.5 Configuration SoT — the only thing SATOM calls a source of truth

The versioned history of every managed appliance's configuration. Each harvest is hashed; an unchanged config writes nothing at all, only a newer last_seen_at, so the version count is a count of real changes. Snapshots are stored content-addressed under data/sot/objects/ with the index in Postgres, replicated to the standby node by satom-ha-datasync, and carried inside every system backup bundle. device_sync and device_inspect are the actions that feed it (§15). The design is in source-of-truth-spec.md.

What does not count as a change

Some values in a harvest move without anyone changing the configuration. They are left out of the version, so they never raise Config drift:

  • the appliance's own clock (only inside the object that carries it — time zone and NTP settings next to it still count);
  • the order of reverse-reference lists, FortiWeb's rolling cookie allow-time, internal numeric handles (*_val next to their name) and FortiWeb's echo of the last sub-table edit (sub_table_*);
  • FortiADC live state: availability of virtual servers, pools and interfaces, and the computed status (OK, Expired) of local, CA and intermediate CA certificates. The configured state beside them — a virtual server's enable/disable/maintain, a certificate's validity dates — still counts, and so does status in every other table.

When one of these rules is added, the newest version of each device is re-keyed in place on its next sync: no new version, no alert.

Two lifetimes: the snapshot and the change log

Since 2026-08-30 these are two different things and each has its own window. The snapshot is the harvested configuration itself and it is large; the change log is the one-line-per-version record an operator walks back through to find the value a parameter used to have, and it is roughly a thousand times smaller. Neither is ever deleted from this node before the backup server has been confirmed to hold it.

The change log is never thrown away — it is moved. Whole past calendar months are written to the backup server as one plain JSONL file per device and month under <system_path>/sot-log/, and the rows leave the database only after that file has been listed back at the exact size that was written. Every field of every row is in the file, so it is a record on its own and can be pulled straight off the backup server with sftp — no restore of the database required.

Why whole months, never part of one. Archiving the old half of a month means writing that month's file again later with fewer rows in it, which would replace a complete archive with a truncated one. A month is therefore archived only once it lies entirely beyond the window, and a file already on the server is never overwritten: a name present at a different size holds the month and says so.

Why a month is also held when its snapshots are still local. Deleting a row whose blob has not gone off-box orphans that blob, and the orphan sweep then deletes it — the archive would point at bytes that exist nowhere. One such row holds its whole month.

Do not expect this to free disk. A row plus its indexes costs ~875 B where the snapshot it points at costs ~62 KB gzipped: a hundred devices changing daily add ~32 MB of rows a year against ~2 GB of payload. The window exists so the table is bounded and the log is provably off-box, not as a space measure — which is why the default is a year and why shortening it to days buys almost nothing while costing the ability to open a device history without going to the network.

This replaces a stricter rule, deliberately. Until 2026-08-30 the index had no setting at all, on the grounds that a knob whose only effect is erasing the record is not a policy. That still holds for a knob that only deletes; the operator asked for the missing half — a window here and the rest off-box, retrievable — and the archive is what makes the shortening safe.

Until this change prune() deleted rows, and that was the documented behaviour. Nothing failed: the page rendered, the suite was green. It only became a data-loss defect the moment a one-day local policy was asked for — the whole history would have gone inside a day while every byte sat safely on the backup server, unreachable, because load() and diff() only ever opened the local file. diff() said so out loud: blob missing (pruned?).

The payload — the gzip snapshot under data/sot/objects/ — leaves. Two numbers govern it, and they are a union, not a pair of caps: a snapshot stays on this node while it is inside the newest N for its device or younger than D days. Defaults: 2 versions and 1 day.

Two, not one, for the versions floor: a diff needs a version and the one before it, and what changed in the last harvest is the most-used view in the product — at one, that view would go to the network every single time.

Days of change log kept in the database is the third field on each card. Default 365, maximum 36500, and 0 is a real value here — unlike the two payload boxes it means never trim, so the whole log stays on this node. (For the payload boxes zero is meaningless: it would evacuate even the newest snapshot, so it reads as unset.) A blank box is still "I did not choose" and restores the default.

These numbers are set per ADOM, and only for ADOMs that are switched on. The panel shows the house rule first and then one card per active ADOM. Resolution is three deep — ADOM key, house key, product default — and each card prints which level answered, because "2 because you set it" and "2 because nobody set anything" lead to different next actions. Leaving all three boxes of an ADOM card empty and saving clears that override so the ADOM inherits again; that is the only way to undo one.

An inactive ADOM has no card. A family switched off in the ADOM registry is off across the whole console — its routes 404, it is gone from the selector — so offering a retention form for it invites tuning a family this node does not manage. But a rule written before it was switched off keeps resolving for every row still filed under that family, so hiding the form must not hide the rule: inactive ADOMs that still carry an override or still hold change-log rows are listed underneath, with the numbers and a Clear the override button. Saving is accepted for any registered ADOM, active or not, precisely so that button can work. Per ADOM because the families are not comparable: a FortiAnalyzer snapshot measures ~6 MB raw where a FortiWeb's is ~0.5 MB, so one number for all four fits none of them.

A 0, a blank or a malformed value means unset and restores the default, never "keep nothing" — zero down this path would evacuate the newest payload too, and the very next diff would go to the network for a config harvested a minute ago.

Confirm off-box, then delete — in that order, always

Evacuation uploads first, lists the server, and deletes locally only what that listing confirms. A listing that fails yields an empty set, so an unreachable or misconfigured server evacuates nothing; it is never read as permission to delete. This ordering is the single line the whole feature rests on, and it is checked per blob, not per server: one file missing from an otherwise healthy listing is kept.

An evacuated version is not gone. Opening it — history, diff, restore — fetches the blob back from the backup server on demand and re-caches it locally, after verifying that the bytes hash to the name they were stored under. The row carries evacuated_at so the page can say where the payload currently lives, and a device that reverts to an older configuration re-writes the blob and clears that flag.

This normally runs by itself after each off-box sync (device_inspect). The Free space on this node now card on this pane does the same thing immediately — its button reads Upload and free space now.

It was called "Apply the payload policy now" / "Push and evacuate now" until 2026-08-30 and nobody could tell from the page whether it deleted their history. It does not. The card now names the two things it removes locally — snapshots the server is confirmed to hold, and change-log months the server is confirmed to hold — and states plainly that nothing is discarded: an evacuated snapshot is fetched back when opened, and an archived month is a file on the backup server. It also prints where the archive lands and what the last run did. A shared snapshot — the same configuration recorded under a chassis and its per-ADOM rows — only leaves when no retained row anywhere still wants it on disk.

Blobs no version references at all are still deleted outright; those are orphans, not history.

Refresh frequency — how often every managed appliance is read and its configuration hashed, in minutes. Default 60, allowed 5 – 10080 (a week); out-of-range values are clamped rather than rejected, because the field has no error channel of its own and a silently dropped value would leave the old number on screen looking saved. A 0, a blank or a malformed value means unset and restores the default — never "harvest never".

This field does not create a settings key. The cadence already has an author: device_sync is the scheduled action that reads a device and mints a version (§15), so a key of its own would be a second author of one number — the panel would show one interval while the scheduler fired on another, and neither would be wrong about itself. The field reads and writes that schedule row, and recomputes its next fire: a stored interval that leaves next_run alone does not apply until the fire that was already pending goes off, which is a setting that looks saved and is inert.

Two consequences worth knowing before typing a small number:

  • A short interval costs device calls, not storage — an unchanged harvest writes nothing at all.
  • The panel names the row it drives and links to it, says whether that row is disabled (in which case nothing is harvested on a schedule at all), and reports any other device_sync schedules it is deliberately not touching. A harvest pinned to a wall-clock time ("every night at 02:00") is a different statement; converting it to an interval would discard it, so it is reported and left alone. If no scheduled harvest exists at all, saving creates one, fleet-wide, at the interval typed.
  • Uploading the new SoT blobs off-box is a separate action on its own schedule (device_inspect) and is edited in Automation, not here.

26.5b Backup Server — the external SFTP destination

The box three separate streams are copied to. It is a destination, not an authority: nothing stored there is consulted to decide what a device is configured to do — that is §26.5.

Stream Written by Path
Device config backups the appliances themselves, on their own schedule (config system backup) Config backups path
System bundles this node's scheduled system-backup action, via push_server (§15), at the hour set on this same pane System bundles path
Firmware archive images retired from local storage Firmware archive path

SATOM connects read-mostly: it inventories what it finds on the System Backup page, diffs device backups against each other, and pulls firmware for console-driven restores. It does not author the device backups — if an appliance stops pushing, SATOM can report the gap but cannot fill it.
